moves.name: Squash and stretch
moves.summary: An object flattens on impact and lengthens in fast travel while keeping its volume, so it reads as soft, alive and pulled by gravity.
moves.body:
Squash and stretch is the oldest trick for making a shape feel like it has mass. A ball lengthens along its direction of travel when it moves fast, flattens against the floor on contact, then springs back to round. The eye reads the deformation as weight and softness long before it reads the geometry.

The rule that makes it work is **volume preservation**: if the shape grows 30 percent on one axis, it shrinks on the other so the area stays about the same. `scaleX = 1 / scaleY` is a good starting point.

It works best on:

- mascots, dots, balls and blobs
- buttons and chips that get pressed or land
- playful brands where a little rubber is welcome

Common mistakes:

- scaling from the center instead of the contact point, so the ball floats above the floor while it squashes
- stretching on the screen axis instead of along the velocity
- deforming text, logos or product UI that must stay legible
- holding the squash too long; two to four frames on contact is plenty

moves.name: Anticipation
moves.summary: A small move in the opposite direction before the main action, like a crouch before a jump, so the viewer knows something is about to happen.
moves.body:
Anticipation is the small opposite move that comes before the real one. A character crouches before it jumps, a card dips 6 px before it flies up, a logo shrinks a hair before it pops. It tells the viewer where to look and makes the main action feel powered instead of teleported.

The size of the wind-up sets the energy. A barely visible dip reads as precise and product-like; a deep, slow crouch reads as cartoon. The wind-up is usually slower than the action it sets up: the crouch eases in, the release snaps.

Use it for:

- jumps, launches and throws
- elements that leave the frame fast
- big reveals you want the audience ready for

Common mistakes:

- wind-ups on every element, which makes the whole film feel hesitant
- a wind-up as big as the action, which reads as a stutter
- a fast exit with no wind-up at all, which can look like a dropped frame
- adding anticipation to text the viewer is still reading

moves.name: Overshoot and settle
moves.summary: An element travels slightly past its resting place and eases back, giving arrivals a sense of momentum instead of a dead stop.
moves.body:
An object with momentum does not stop exactly where it is going. Overshoot lets it pass the target by a few percent and come back, so the arrival has a little life. In code this is either an `easeOutBack` curve or an underdamped spring.

How much is the whole decision. A rough budget by tone:

- premium or editorial: none
- confident product: 0 to 3 percent
- friendly: 4 to 8 percent
- playful or kids: 8 to 17 percent

Overshoot is punctuation. Put it on the hero, or on the last item of a group so it marks the moment the group is complete. Scale overshoot reads more strongly than position overshoot, so use about half as much on scale.

Common mistakes:

- overshoot on everything, which turns a product film into a toy
- springing opacity, which clips above 1 and makes the fade look cut off
- scaling up from 0, which passes through tiny unreadable sizes; start at 0.85 or higher
- wobble that is still visible while the viewer tries to read

moves.name: Follow-through and overlapping action
moves.summary: Loose parts of an object start moving after the body and keep going after it stops, so a move reads as one physical thing instead of a rigid block.
moves.body:
When a body stops, the loose parts attached to it keep going for a moment: hair, a tail, a cape, a shadow, a label hanging under a card. When the body starts, those parts start late. That offset is follow-through and overlapping action, and it is what separates a rigid move from a physical one.

In code it is cheap. Run the attached part on the same curve as the body with a delay of 2 to 6 frames, or on a softer spring so it trails and catches up. Each step further from the body gets a little more lag.

Good places for it:

- UI cards with labels, badges or shadows
- characters with limbs, ears or antennas
- tab indicators whose back edge catches up with the front edge

Common mistakes:

- lag so long that the parts look disconnected
- every part on the same delay, which reads as a second block arriving late
- trailing parts that wobble far more than the body, which looks like jelly
- splitting up text lines that need to be read together

moves.name: Spring animation
moves.summary: Motion driven by a damped spring instead of a fixed curve, tuned with stiffness, damping and mass, so arrivals feel physical and consistent.
moves.body:
A spring moves a value toward its target the way a weight on a spring would. Instead of choosing a duration and a curve, you choose **stiffness** (how hard it pulls), **damping** (how quickly it calms down) and **mass** (how heavy it feels). One set of numbers then handles arrivals, presses and interruptions with the same physics.

The number that predicts the feel is the damping ratio, `damping / (2 × √(stiffness × mass))`. Near 1 the value lands firmly with no wobble. Around 0.6 it overshoots once and settles. Below 0.4 it rings like a cartoon.

Springs suit anything that should feel physical. Use a cubic-bezier instead when a move must finish on an exact frame, like a wipe that lands on a beat.

Common mistakes:

- mixing several spring personalities in one scene, so objects seem to come from different worlds
- restarting a spring from zero velocity when its target changes, which leaves a visible kink
- forgetting that a spring has no fixed end; compute its settle time before placing it on a cue

moves.name: Staggered timing
moves.summary: A group of items runs the same animation with small start offsets, so the group arrives as one directional ripple instead of all at once.
moves.body:
Stagger takes one animation and starts it at slightly different times for each item in a group. Cards, list rows, words or logos cascade in, and the group reads as a single gesture with a direction.

Typical offsets:

- words in a headline: 60 to 120 ms
- cards and tiles: 80 to 160 ms
- many small items, like a logo wall: 40 to 80 ms

Keep the whole cascade under about 0.8 s. Past that, shrink the offset or reveal in chunks. Order follows meaning: reading order for text, importance for features, center-out for radial layouts.

Common mistakes:

- offsets below two frames, which read as simultaneous anyway
- a perfectly even ladder across a dozen items, which looks generated; group them in phrases like 2 + 3 + 2
- varying the easing per item; keep the curve and duration identical and vary only the start time
- exits that stagger as slowly as entrances; use half the offset, or exit all at once

moves.name: Slow in and slow out
moves.summary: A move starts gently, gathers speed in the middle and decelerates into its stop. The default for anything traveling between two on-screen points.
moves.body:
Real objects do not jump to full speed or stop dead. Slow in and slow out spaces the frames tightly at the start and end of a move and widely in the middle, so the object accelerates, travels, then decelerates. In code that is an ease-in-out curve: `cubic-bezier(0.83, 0, 0.17, 1)` for a strong quint shape, or a sine in-out for something gentler.

Use it when something moves between two places that are both on screen:

- camera pushes, pans and pulls
- a card rearranging into a new layout
- wipes and panels that cross the frame

The steepness of the curve is the character. A gentle sine feels calm and expensive; a steep quint feels decisive.

Common mistakes:

- `linear` on anything except constant-speed motion such as tickers and rotation loops
- ease-in-out on entrances, which makes them arrive sluggishly; entrances should only decelerate
- a steep curve on a slow two-second camera move, which makes the middle feel rushed
- the same duration for short and long moves; longer travel needs more time

moves.name: Ease-out entrance
moves.summary: Elements arrive fast and decelerate into place, then leave by accelerating away, so entrances feel confident and exits get out of the way.
moves.body:
The single most useful easing rule: things that **arrive** decelerate, things that **leave** accelerate. An entrance on an exponential ease-out covers most of its distance in the first third of its duration, then glides into place. The viewer sees motion immediately and gets a calm landing to read.

A good default is `cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)`. Exits use the mirror, an ease-in like `cubic-bezier(0.7, 0, 0.84, 0)`, take 60 to 75 percent of the entrance time and travel less.

It reads well for:

- headlines, cards and panels entering
- anything that needs a readable resting state soon after it appears

Common mistakes:

- ease-in entrances, which make the element feel late and then slam into place
- ease-out exits, which make leaving elements linger and compete with what comes next
- exits as long as entrances, which slows the whole film down
- animating an exit at all when the scene is about to cut; let the cut do it

moves.name: Arcs
moves.summary: Moving objects follow curved paths rather than straight lines, the way thrown balls, swinging limbs and real hands on a mouse do.
moves.body:
Almost nothing in the physical world travels in a straight line. A thrown object follows a parabola, a limb swings around a joint, a hand moving a mouse traces a soft curve. Motion on arcs reads as natural; motion on straight lines between keyframes reads as computed.

In code, an arc usually comes from animating x and y on different curves. Run x on a gentle ease and y on an ease-out going up and an ease-in coming down, and the path bends into a parabola. For a cursor, put one bezier control point off the straight line by 10 to 20 percent of the distance.

Where it matters most:

- jumps, throws and landings
- cursors traveling between buttons
- logos or dots that fly to a new position

Common mistakes:

- interpolating x and y together on one curve, which always gives a straight line
- arcs that bend against gravity for no reason
- arcs that bend to a different side on every move, which looks random
- huge arcs on UI elements, which turns a precise move into a cartoon

moves.name: Moving hold
moves.summary: During a pause the frame keeps a trace of motion, like a 2 percent push-in or a slow drift, so a held moment never looks frozen.
moves.body:
A hold is where the viewer actually reads. But a frame where nothing moves at all looks like the video stalled. A moving hold keeps a tiny amount of motion running while everything important stays put: a 1 to 3 percent push-in, a slow background drift, a gentle scale breath on a logo.

The motion has to be slow enough not to compete. Run it at a steady speed across the whole hold, and keep it on the camera or the background, not on the text being read.

It works for:

- the hold right after a big reveal
- end lockups and calls to action
- stats or quotes that need several seconds on screen

Common mistakes:

- drift fast enough that the eye follows it instead of reading
- easing the drift in and out inside the hold, which makes the frame pulse
- holding before the big moment instead of after it; the longest hold belongs right after the peak
- cutting a hold below the read floor: one to three words need at least 0.8 s fully settled

moves.name: Secondary action
moves.summary: A smaller supporting motion that happens with the main one, like a blink during a hop or neighbors nudging aside when a card lands.
moves.body:
Secondary action is a small extra motion that supports the main one without competing with it. A character hops and its eyes glance at a light; a card lands and its neighbors nudge 4 to 8 px aside; a button is pressed and a ring spreads from it. The scene feels connected because things respond to each other.

Two rules keep it honest: the secondary motion is **smaller** than the main action, and it comes **later**, usually as the main action lands. If it is as big or as early, the viewer no longer knows which move matters.

It works for:

- landings and clicks, where the world can react
- mascots and characters, through blinks, glances and breathing
- dashboards, where a changing number can tint its label

Common mistakes:

- secondary motion that starts before the main action and steals the focus
- reactions on everything in the frame
- reactions on a different spring or curve family from the rest of the film

moves.name: Animating on twos
moves.summary: Each pose is held for two or more frames, giving smooth code-driven motion the stepped, hand-made cadence of cel animation or stop motion.
moves.body:
Code animation is perfectly smooth by default, which can make it feel synthetic. Animating on twos holds each pose for two frames, so a 24 fps film shows 12 new poses per second. On threes or fours it gets choppier and more handmade. Paper, pencil, crayon and pixel styles look far more convincing with this stepped cadence.

Nothing needs redrawing. Compute the animation as usual, then quantize time before sampling it: `t = floor(frame / 2) * 2 / fps`. Line boil, where hand-drawn strokes jitter slightly on each new pose, is the same trick applied to a noise seed.

It works for:

- hand-drawn, paper and collage looks
- pixel art and sprite-style loops
- character moments inside an otherwise smooth film, for contrast

Common mistakes:

- stepping the camera as well, which turns a smooth pan into a stutter
- stepping text that should stay perfectly stable
- mixing stepped and smooth layers without a clear rule, so it reads as dropped frames

moves.name: Staggered letter reveal
moves.summary: A word appears one character at a time, each letter rising and fading in a few frames after the one before it, so the word ripples into place.
moves.body:
Each character is its own layer. They all run the same short entrance (a rise, a fade, sometimes a small scale), but each one starts a fixed delay after its neighbour. The eye reads it as a wave travelling through the word rather than twelve separate events.

It works best on **one short word or a name**: a brand reveal, a title card, the hero word of a scene. Past about 20 characters the wave takes too long and the viewer waits for the end before they can read it.

- Keep the per-letter move small. A 20 to 40 px rise is enough; big travel turns into noise.
- Use a total spread, not just a delay. Decide that the whole word lands in 400 to 600 ms and divide by the letter count.
- Lay out the full word first, then animate letters in their final slots. Never let kerning or centering shift while letters arrive.
- Do not mix directions. If letters come up from below, every letter comes up from below.

The common mistake is easing each letter linearly. Give every letter a strong ease-out so each one decelerates into place.

moves.name: Word by word reveal
aka: one word at a time text
moves.summary: A sentence builds one word at a time, each word rising out of a light blur into its final slot, paced to the voice or the beat.
moves.body:
The line is laid out in full but invisible. Words then switch on one after another, each with a quick rise and fade, sometimes out of a soft blur. Because the reader gets one word per beat, the sentence feels spoken even without audio.

Use it for **headlines, punchlines, voiceover captions and manifesto lines**. It is the default for sentences, where a per-letter stagger would be too slow and too busy.

- Space words 60 to 120 ms apart for a brisk read; match exact word timestamps when there is a voice.
- Reserve every word's position first. A line that re-centres as it grows looks broken.
- Give the key word something extra: a later arrival, the accent colour, or a slightly longer hold before the next word.
- Hold the finished line long enough to read twice before it leaves.

The usual mistakes are wrapping a long sentence onto four lines (split it into cards instead) and timing words evenly when the voice does not speak evenly. Short words like "a" and "the" can arrive together with the word after them.

moves.name: Typewriter text
moves.summary: Text types itself out character by character behind a caret, with an uneven human rhythm, like someone entering a prompt or a search query.
moves.body:
Characters appear one at a time at the end of the line, led by a caret. Nothing moves or fades; a character is either there or not. That plainness is the point: the viewer reads it as input, as something being typed right now.

It fits **prompts, search bars, chat messages, code and terminal scenes**. It is wrong for anything the viewer must read instantly, because the message only exists once typing finishes.

- Type at 20 to 40 characters per second, and break the rhythm: short pauses after spaces and punctuation, an occasional two-character burst.
- Derive visible characters from time (`floor(progress * length)`), so scrubbing and rendering are deterministic.
- Left-align the text so the start never moves as the line grows.
- The caret stays solid while typing and blinks only while idle, at about 530 ms per phase.

Mistakes: perfectly even spacing (reads robotic), fading each character in (reads as a reveal, not typing), and typing a long paragraph the viewer gives up on. Pair it with soft key clicks if there is sound.

moves.name: Text scramble decode
moves.summary: Each letter flickers through random glyphs before locking onto the right character, left to right, so the word appears to decode itself.
moves.body:
Every character slot cycles through random symbols for a short while, then settles on its real letter. Slots resolve in order, usually left to right, so a readable word spreads across a field of noise. It reads as computation: data resolving, a password cracking, a signal coming through.

Use it for **tech brands, data products, labels and short titles**. Keep it to one line. On a paragraph it is unreadable and tiring.

- Use a monospace font, or fix each slot's width, so shuffling glyphs never make the line jitter sideways.
- Pick the noise set on purpose: uppercase plus a few symbols looks cleaner than the full ASCII range.
- Change glyphs every 2 frames at 30 fps, not every frame. Every-frame flicker turns to grey mush.
- Seed the randomness so every render produces the same frames.

The common mistake is resolving every letter at once at the end. The left-to-right lock is what makes it readable. A second mistake is leaving resolved letters still flickering.

moves.name: Line mask text reveal
moves.summary: Each line of text slides up from behind an invisible edge, as if rising out of a slot in the page, then stops dead on its baseline.
moves.body:
Each line sits inside a clipping box the height of the line. The text starts fully below the box and slides up into view, so it seems to emerge from a hard edge rather than fade in. It looks precise and editorial, and it hides the fact that anything moved.

It suits **headlines, credits, editorial layouts and calm product films**. It is the cleanest way to bring in two or three lines without any blur or opacity.

- Make the mask about 1.15 times the line height with extra room at the bottom, or descenders get clipped.
- Travel the full line height. A half-height rise shows the cut-off top of the letters at the start.
- Use a strong ease-out, around 500 to 700 ms per line, and offset lines by 80 to 120 ms.
- Exit the same way: lines lift out through the top of the mask.

Mistakes: adding a fade on top (it muddies the hard edge), a loose mask that reveals the text before it crosses the line, and different line heights on one card so lines arrive at uneven speeds.

moves.name: Variable font weight animation
moves.summary: A word swells from hairline thin to heavy black (or back) by animating a variable font's weight axis, so the letters themselves change shape.
moves.body:
Instead of moving the text, you change its anatomy. A variable font exposes axes such as weight (`wght`) and width (`wdth`), and animating them makes strokes thicken or letters widen in place. A word that grows from 100 to 900 weight feels like it is gaining force.

It works for **emphasis on one word, playful identities, beat hits and breathing loops**. It is subtle and typographic, so it suits brands that would never use a bounce.

- Only use fonts that ship the axis. Faking it with stroke width or scale looks wrong immediately.
- Weight changes widen the word. Anchor it left or right, or animate width in the opposite direction to hold the footprint.
- Ease it like a physical push: fast into the heavy weight, slow back out.
- For a wave, offset the weight per letter by 30 to 50 ms.

The common mistake is letting the line reflow as the weight grows, shoving every word after it. Lay the line out at its heaviest state, or isolate the animated word in its own box with a fixed width.

moves.name: Text on a path
moves.summary: A line of text runs along a curve, circle or wave and slides along it, so the words travel the shape like a train on a track.
moves.body:
The text is set on a path instead of a straight baseline: a circle, an arc, a wave, the outline of a product. Animating the start offset along the path makes the words crawl around the shape. A ring of text slowly turning around a logo or a badge is the classic case.

Use it for **badges, stickers, end cards, loops and decorative frames** around a hero object. It is supporting type, not the main message: curved text is slower to read.

- Keep the phrase short and repeat it with a separator (a dot or a star) so a closed ring has no gap.
- Move slowly. One full turn every 8 to 12 seconds reads; faster becomes a blur.
- On tight curves, increase tracking a little so letters on the inside do not collide.
- For a seamless loop, make the total offset over the loop exactly one path length.

Mistakes: putting the key message on a curve, using a path with sharp corners (letters fold and overlap), and letting the text run upside down at the bottom of a circle where it matters.

moves.name: Rotating word swap
moves.summary: One word inside a fixed headline rolls vertically to the next option and the next, while the rest of the sentence stays perfectly still.
moves.body:
A headline like "Made for designers" keeps its frame, and only the last word changes: designers, founders, teams. The outgoing word slides up and out of a mask while the new one slides up from below. The still part of the line anchors the eye, so the swap reads as a list without showing a list.

It is made for **audience lists, feature lists, use cases and time or status changes**.

- Each swap takes 350 to 500 ms; hold each word at least long enough to read it twice, around 700 ms or more.
- Mask the swap slot so words never overlap the static text.
- When the words differ in width, either left-align the slot or animate the slot width alongside the roll so the sentence does not jump.
- Keep the direction constant. Up and out, up and in, every time.

Mistakes: swapping faster than anyone can read, letting the whole line re-centre on every word, and cycling more than five or six words. Land on the final word with a slightly longer roll and a firm stop.

moves.name: Split-flap text
moves.summary: Letters flip like an old airport departure board, each tile rattling through the alphabet before it lands on the right character.
moves.body:
Each character sits on a tile split horizontally in the middle. To change, the top half falls forward and reveals the next character, over and over, until the tile reaches its target. Tiles finish at different times, so the board settles in a ragged wave.

It suits **travel, schedules, countdowns, launch dates, scores and retro product themes**. The mechanical motion says "live update" in a way a fade never does.

- Each flip is short, around 60 to 90 ms, with the falling half accelerating as it drops.
- Darken the falling half as it tilts and add a thin gap line between halves; that shading sells the hinge.
- Give each tile a different number of flips so they land at staggered moments.
- Use a monospace or tabular font so tiles stay a fixed size.

Mistakes: flipping the whole tile as one card (it reads as a turn, not a flap), every tile stopping on the same frame, and running it on long text. Six to sixteen characters is the comfortable range. Pair each flip with a tiny click if there is sound.

moves.name: Scale punch headline
moves.summary: A headline hits the screen oversized, snaps down past its final size and settles with a small spring, landing like a punch on the beat.
moves.body:
The word appears big, around 120 to 140 percent, and compresses into place in a few frames, overshooting slightly below full size before springing back. The fast shrink reads as impact. It is the type version of a drum hit.

Use it for **hooks, punchlines, short promo lines and beat drops**. One or two words per punch; it does not work on a sentence.

- Make the hit fast: 150 to 250 ms from first frame to rest, with most of the change in the first third.
- Keep overshoot small, about 3 to 6 percent. Big wobble makes the word unreadable while it settles.
- Land the moment of contact exactly on the beat or the stressed syllable, not the start of the move.
- Sell it with a companion: a one-frame flash, a short camera nudge, or a thud.

Mistakes: punching every line in a video (it stops meaning anything), scaling single letters inside a word, and scaling from the centre when the text is left-aligned. Set the transform origin to where the text is anchored.

moves.name: Tracking expand title
moves.summary: A title fades in with its letters slowly drifting apart, letter-spacing easing from tight to wide over several seconds, like a film opening.
moves.body:
Only the space between letters animates. The title appears tight and spreads gently outward while it fades in, sometimes continuing to drift for the whole time it is on screen. It is slow, quiet and confident: the classic film-title move.

It fits **cinematic titles, trailers, luxury or calm brands and chapter cards**. It needs time, so give it at least 2 to 4 seconds of screen life.

- Use uppercase, which tolerates wide tracking. Lowercase falls apart when spread.
- Animate tracking from a small negative value to a moderate positive one, for example 0 to 0.3 em, never to absurd widths.
- Keep the centre fixed. The title should grow outward from the middle, not slide right.
- Use a slow ease-out, or keep a very slow linear drift after the fade so the shot never feels frozen.

Mistakes: animating it fast (it looks like a glitch), using it on body text, and letting the final width break out of the safe area. Lay out the end state first and check it fits.

moves.name: Outline to fill text
moves.summary: Letters first draw themselves as thin outlines, then fill in with solid colour, so a word goes from blueprint to finished type.
moves.body:
The move has two beats. First the letter outlines draw on, the stroke tracing each glyph's contour. Then the fill floods in, by fading, by wiping up from the baseline, or letter by letter. The viewer sees the word being constructed before it becomes solid.

It suits **logo and wordmark reveals, design or engineering brands, and "from idea to product" stories**. It needs large display type; outlines on small text vanish.

- Convert the text to paths so each glyph has a stroke you can draw with a dash offset.
- Draw all letters together or with a 40 to 60 ms stagger, over 600 to 900 ms.
- Start the fill only after the outline is complete, with a short beat of 100 to 200 ms between them.
- Keep the stroke the same colour as the fill so the fill looks like it grows from the line, then drop the stroke once filled.

Mistakes: a stroke so thin it disappears on a phone, drawing glyphs from random start points (pick a consistent start per letter), and filling before the outline closes, which makes it look like a loading error.

moves.name: Match cut
moves.summary: A hard cut between two shots that share a shape, color or position, so the eye carries straight across and the change feels intended.
moves.body:
A match cut is a plain cut with one thing held constant across it: a circle becomes a button, a horizon becomes a divider line, a word in the same spot becomes another word. The viewer's eye is already parked on that shape, so the new shot arrives without a search.

It works best when the two shots are different things that rhyme, and when the cut lands on a beat or mid-action. It costs zero screen time, which makes it the strongest option when a film is short on seconds.

Common mistakes:

- **Alignment drift.** A few pixels of offset in position or size reads as a mistake. Compare the frame before and after the cut side by side.
- Matching shapes that are too small to register. The shared element should be the dominant shape in both frames.
- Cutting between two still frames. Keep something moving through the cut so it reads as one gesture.
- Using it every scene. Three or four good matches per film are enough.

moves.name: Whip pan transition
moves.summary: The outgoing shot snaps sideways into a directional blur and the next shot decelerates in from the same direction, hiding the cut in the smear.
moves.body:
A whip pan fakes a camera flicking so fast that the picture smears. The cut sits inside the blurriest frames, so the viewer never sees it. It reads as energy and momentum, a jump to the next idea without a pause.

Use it between sections that belong to the same world, on a beat, ideally with a short whoosh whose peak lands on the cut frame. A vertical version (whip tilt) works well for scrolling into a new page or panel.

Common mistakes:

- **Mismatched direction.** If the outgoing shot leaves to the left, the incoming one must arrive moving left too, or the motion reverses and jolts.
- Blur on every frame. Apply directional blur only during the fastest part of the move; the start and the settle should be sharp.
- Symmetric timing. The exit should accelerate hard and the entry should spend longer decelerating.
- Whipping every two seconds. It loses its punch fast; save it for jumps in energy.

moves.name: Wipe transition
moves.summary: A moving edge sweeps across the frame, revealing the next shot behind it, often with a thin accent-colored line leading the reveal.
moves.body:
A wipe replaces one shot with another along a moving edge: a straight line, a diagonal, a clock hand, or a brand shape. It openly says "new section" without the softness of a fade, which suits chapter breaks, list items and before/after comparisons.

It looks designed rather than default when the edge has character. A thin accent-colored bar or line that runs a few frames ahead of the reveal edge gives the eye something to follow and hides any aliasing on the mask.

Common mistakes:

- **Linear speed.** A constant-speed wipe looks like a 1990s slideshow. Use an in-out curve unless you want a deliberately mechanical look.
- Wiping against the film's direction of travel. If time moves left to right, keep wipes moving the same way every time.
- Soft, feathered edges at large sizes. They read as a smudge; keep the edge crisp or use a clear leading line.
- Mixing three wipe shapes in one film.

moves.name: Iris transition
moves.summary: A circle or aperture closes down on a point of the frame and opens again onto the next shot, centred on the same spot.
moves.body:
An iris shrinks the visible picture to a point, then opens it onto something new. Because the closing point is chosen, it doubles as a pointer: the last thing you see is the button, face or product you want remembered, and the next shot opens from the same place.

A plain circle reads playful and cartoon-like. A bladed camera aperture reads mechanical and premium, and suits photo, camera and hardware products. Both work well on a strong beat, closing just before it and snapping open on it.

Common mistakes:

- **Closing on nothing.** Center the iris on the subject, not on the frame center by default.
- Leaving it fully closed too long. Two to four frames of black is plenty; more feels like a stall.
- Opening too small. The final radius must reach past the farthest frame corner, or corners stay masked for a frame.
- Using a soft feathered circle, which looks like a vignette rather than a transition.

moves.name: Morph transition
moves.summary: One element persists across two scenes and glides from its old size, position and color into its new one while the rest of the scene changes around it.
moves.body:
A morph transition carries one shared element from scene A into scene B: a card becomes a page, a pill becomes a toolbar, a word becomes a logo. Nothing is replaced; the viewer watches one thing change, so continuity is built into the edit.

It is the backbone of continuous-take product films and app demos, where every scene should grow out of the previous one. Interpolate position, size, corner radius and color together on one curve, and let the destination scene's supporting elements arrive after the traveller is most of the way there.

Common mistakes:

- **Guessed coordinates.** Measure the element's box in both scenes; an off landing creates a visible pop on the last frame.
- Animating font size, which shimmers. Scale the element and swap to the real text on the landing frame.
- Morphing two things that have no relationship. Use a match cut or push instead.
- Everything arriving at once with the traveller.

moves.name: Color flood transition
moves.summary: A shape grows out of an element in the frame until its color covers the screen, then becomes the next scene's background or shrinks into its next element.
moves.body:
A color flood turns a small element, usually a button, dot or card, into the whole frame. It reads as "this thing opens up into the next idea", which is why it pairs naturally with a click or a beat drop. The flood can hold as the next scene's background, or contract into a different element and hand the story on.

Use the element's own shape (circle, pill, rounded rectangle) so the growth feels like the object expanding, not a generic wipe. A copy of the button's label can ride on top of the flood and land as the next title.

Common mistakes:

- **Stopping at the frame edge.** The shape must grow past the farthest corner, or corners stay uncovered for a frame.
- Too slow. Much past a third of a second reads as a fade rather than a burst.
- Stacking bugs: an outgoing layer floating above the flood. Set layer order explicitly.
- Full-frame accent floods every scene, which overloads the palette.

moves.name: Zoom-through transition
moves.summary: The camera pushes into a detail with accelerating scale until it fills the frame, then the next scene settles in from inside it.
moves.body:
A zoom-through dives into one detail of the current shot (a tile, a pixel, a word, a dot) until the detail becomes the whole screen, and the next scene starts from there. It says "look closer" and reads like going one level deeper into a product or story.

The key is an exponential scale ramp: scale doubling at a steady rate feels like constant speed, while a linear scale ramp feels like it stalls and then lurches. Hand off at the moment the detail fills the frame, with the incoming scene starting slightly oversized and easing down to rest.

Common mistakes:

- **Linear scale interpolation.** Interpolate in log space.
- Zooming into tiny or blank points, which produces a few frames of meaningless blur.
- Zooming in and immediately back out. Pick a direction and keep it.
- Rasterized content. Scaling bitmap UI 20x shows pixels; render vector or high-res sources at the deep end.

moves.name: Push transition
moves.summary: The outgoing shot slides off one edge while the incoming shot slides on behind it, both moving together like pages on a strip.
moves.body:
In a push, both shots move as one strip: the old one leaves as the new one arrives, with no gap. It reads as "next, in the same space", like swiping pages or moving along a timeline, so it suits sequences such as feature lists, stats and onboarding steps.

A small scale-down on the outgoing shot adds depth, and a little directional blur during the fastest middle of the move adds speed without smearing the readable frames.

Common mistakes:

- **Inconsistent direction.** Pick one direction of travel for the whole film; new content usually enters from the right.
- Ease-out only. A push needs an in-out curve, or the start jerks.
- Eating the read time. The text on both sides needs its own hold outside the transition duration.
- Generic slide-left on every scene. If every cut is a push, it becomes wallpaper. Mix with hard cuts.

moves.name: Cross-dissolve
moves.summary: Two shots overlap in opacity so one fades through the other, signaling passing time or a change of mood rather than a jump.
moves.body:
A cross-dissolve blends the outgoing and incoming shots over a short overlap. It is the softest transition and means "time passes" or "the feeling shifts". It is also the most overused, which is why many motion directors ban it from product films entirely.

It works when the two shots are calm, related in tone, and the film wants a breath. A blur-dissolve, where both shots pick up a few pixels of blur at the midpoint, hides the double-exposure look. A dip to the background color is a cleaner cousin for chapter breaks.

Common mistakes:

- **The muddy midpoint.** Two busy frames at 50% each look like a mistake. Dissolve between simple compositions.
- Linear opacity on dark-to-light changes, which brightens unevenly. Ease the curve.
- Using it to avoid planning a real transition. If an element could carry over, morph it instead.
- Adding scale, blur and flash on top. Pick one.

moves.name: Glitch cut
moves.summary: One or two frames of digital breakup, like channel split, slice offsets or pixel smear, sit exactly on a cut so the change feels like signal interference.
moves.body:
A glitch cut puts a very short burst of digital damage on the cut point: red and blue channels split apart, horizontal slices offset, blocks smear. It reads as interference, tech, or a hard jump in tone. The effect belongs to the cut, not to the shot, so it should be gone almost before the viewer can name it.

It suits tech launches, music videos and edgy brand bumpers, especially paired with a click or a crunchy sound hit on the same frame.

Common mistakes:

- **Too long.** Past three or four frames it becomes an effect layer instead of a cut.
- Random glitches with no cut behind them. Tie every glitch to a real edit point.
- Breaking readable text. Readable lines should get clean frames before and after the glitch.
- Using a random seed per render. Seed the slice offsets so the result is identical every render.
- Flashing too often; check frequency against photosensitivity limits.

moves.name: Light leak transition
moves.summary: A warm wash of overexposed color blooms across the frame, peaks over the cut point, and fades to reveal the next shot, like light hitting film.
moves.body:
A light leak borrows from film cameras where stray light fogged the frame. A soft gradient of warm color (orange, red, pale yellow) drifts in from an edge, brightens to cover the cut, and fades away. It reads nostalgic, warm and organic, a gentle way to bridge two shots without a hard edge.

It fits travel, lifestyle, music and analog-themed pieces, and works best over footage or photos rather than flat UI.

Common mistakes:

- **Pure white flash.** A full-frame jump to white is a flash, not a leak. Keep the peak tinted and below full brightness, and blend with screen or add.
- Static gradients. A leak should drift and change shape a little while it passes.
- Using it on crisp product UI, where it looks like a filter slapped on top.
- Every cut getting one. One or two per film keeps them special.

moves.name: J-cut and L-cut
moves.summary: The sound of the next scene starts before its picture (J-cut), or the current scene's sound continues after the picture changes (L-cut).
moves.body:
A split edit offsets the audio cut from the picture cut. In a **J-cut**, you hear the next scene first: a voice, a click, the first note of the drop, and the picture follows. In an **L-cut**, the current sound carries over into the next picture. Either way the ear bridges the cut, so the visual change feels motivated instead of abrupt.

In code-made videos this matters most for voiceover and sound design: start the next line of narration or the incoming whoosh a few frames before the scene changes, and the edit stops feeling like slides.

Common mistakes:

- **Offsets that are too long.** A second of mismatched sound feels like a sync error. A few to a dozen frames is usually enough.
- Splitting every cut. Keep some hard, synchronous cuts for impact.
- Letting the carried-over sound clash with the new scene's music. Duck it.
- Splitting visual-sound hits that must land together, like a click on a button.

moves.name: Cursor-led product demo
moves.summary: A synthetic cursor glides across a recreated interface, pauses, clicks and drives each state change so the viewer follows one point of attention.
moves.body:
A cursor-led demo uses a drawn pointer as the narrator. Every change on screen happens because the cursor went somewhere and did something, so the viewer never has to search the frame for what moved.

It reads well when the cursor travels on gentle curves, slows down before it arrives, rests for a few frames, then clicks. That small pause tells the eye "this is the target" before anything reacts.

It works for:

- SaaS launch videos and feature announcements
- Onboarding clips that show one flow end to end
- Social cuts where the UI has to be readable at phone size

Common mistakes:

- Moving in straight lines at constant speed, which looks like a robot replay of a screen recording
- Clicking the instant the cursor lands, so the click and the arrival blur together
- Letting the UI respond before the press finishes
- Wandering paths with no purpose between targets

Keep the cursor slightly larger than real size, and give it a soft shadow so it sits above the interface instead of inside it.

moves.name: Click ripple
moves.summary: On click, the button dips slightly and a soft ring expands from the exact press point and fades, confirming the interaction.
moves.body:
A click ripple is the visual receipt for an action. The button compresses for a moment, and a ring or filled circle grows outward from where the pointer touched, fading as it spreads.

In a video there is no real finger or mouse, so the ripple is what makes a click feel physical. Without it, a state change after a cursor arrives can look accidental.

It works best when:

- The ripple starts at the click point, not the button center
- The press and the ripple begin on the same frame
- The result of the click starts as the ripple is still fading, so cause and effect overlap

Common mistakes:

- Ripples that are too opaque or too large and cover the label
- Using a linear expansion, which looks mechanical; the ring should burst out fast and decelerate
- Adding ripples to every click in a long demo, which turns into noise

A ripple can also grow into the next scene: let it keep expanding until its color fills the frame and becomes the background of what comes next.

moves.name: Auto zoom on click
moves.summary: The whole interface scales up toward the area being used, follows the cursor while it works, then eases back out to show context.
moves.body:
Auto zoom fixes the biggest problem of product footage: a full desktop UI is unreadable on a phone. Instead of showing everything at once, the frame pushes in on the region where the action happens, holds there while the cursor works, and pulls back out once the result needs context.

The zoom should feel like an attentive camera operator. It starts slightly before the cursor reaches its target, settles, and drifts a little with the cursor rather than staying frozen.

It works for:

- Recreated app screens and real screen recordings
- Form filling, typing in a prompt box, toggling settings
- Vertical cuts of desktop products

Common mistakes:

- Zooming on every single click, which causes motion sickness
- Zoom levels above about 2.5x, where text and borders go soft
- Snapping the zoom center to the cursor each frame, which makes the screen jitter
- Zooming out and back in within one second

Group nearby actions under one zoom and only return to the wide view when the location really changes.

moves.name: Card stack
moves.summary: Cards arrive one after another and settle on top of each other with a small offset, shrink and dim, building a layered pile with depth.
moves.body:
A card stack shows several items as a pile instead of a row. Each new card slides or rises in and lands on top, while the cards beneath step back: a little smaller, a little higher, a little darker. The result reads as depth without any 3D camera.

It is a good fit for:

- Feature lists where each card is one benefit
- Testimonials, notifications or messages piling up
- Showing a queue or history of items

The stack only reads if the offsets are consistent. Every card underneath should move by the same step, so the pile looks ordered rather than scattered.

Common mistakes:

- Leaving lower cards at full brightness, so they compete with the top card
- Offsets so small the stack looks like one thick card
- Stacking more than four visible layers; past that, hide the bottom ones
- All cards animating at once, which removes the counting rhythm

To exit, you can fan the stack apart, swipe the top card away to reveal the next, or collapse the whole pile into a single badge.

moves.name: Modal spring-in
moves.summary: A dialog scales up from slightly smaller with a light spring overshoot while the background dims and blurs behind it.
moves.body:
Modal spring-in is how a dialog, popover or bottom sheet enters with weight. The panel starts a little smaller and transparent, grows to full size with a small overshoot, and the page behind it dims so attention moves to the front.

It reads as responsive when the modal grows from the thing that triggered it, such as the button that was clicked, rather than from the screen center.

Use it for:

- Confirmation dialogs, checkout sheets, command palettes
- Showing a detail view without cutting away from the app
- Mobile bottom sheets, using a vertical slide instead of a scale

Common mistakes:

- Starting from scale 0, which looks like a cartoon pop rather than software
- Too much bounce; real interfaces overshoot by a few percent at most
- Dimming the background after the modal lands instead of during
- Content inside the modal appearing at the same instant as the frame

Let the modal's content follow slightly behind the container. Title first, then body, then buttons, so the eye reads it top to bottom.

moves.name: Skeleton to content
moves.summary: Grey placeholder blocks shimmer in the shape of a layout, then real text and images fade in over them block by block.
moves.body:
Skeleton to content shows a screen loading. The layout appears first as rounded grey bars and boxes, a soft highlight sweeps across them, and then real content replaces each block in reading order.

In a video this move is a way to say "it's working" or "it's generating" without a spinner. It also makes the arrival of the real content feel like a payoff.

It works for:

- AI tools generating a result
- Dashboards that fill with data
- Feeds or search results populating

The placeholders must match the final layout. If a grey bar sits where a heading lands, the swap looks intentional; if the shapes do not line up, it looks like a glitch.

Common mistakes:

- Holding the shimmer too long; one or two sweeps are enough in a video
- Replacing everything at once instead of top to bottom
- A shimmer so bright it flickers on compressed social video
- Hard cuts from grey to content with no crossfade

Keep the shimmer subtle and angled slightly, and stagger the reveal so the screen fills like it is arriving from a server.

moves.name: Toast notification
moves.summary: A small notification slides in from a screen edge with a quick spring, holds long enough to read, then slides or shrinks away.
moves.body:
A toast is a short message that confirms an action or announces something new. It enters from an edge, settles with a tiny overshoot, stays still while it is read, and leaves faster than it arrived.

In product videos, toasts are useful as punctuation. After a sequence of clicks, a toast saying "Exported" or "3 new leads" closes the beat and states the result in words.

It works for:

- Confirming the outcome of a demo flow
- Simulated incoming messages or alerts
- Several notifications stacking, with older ones pushed down

Common mistakes:

- Not leaving enough reading time; count roughly 250 ms per word plus a beat
- Entering with a long fade instead of motion, which feels sluggish
- Toasts that cover the very UI element they describe
- Exits slower than entrances

When several arrive, push older toasts down and shrink them slightly so the newest one is always the clearest. Matching the app's real toast style, position and corner radius makes the demo feel authentic.

moves.name: Tab indicator slide
moves.summary: The active tab underline or pill glides to the newly selected tab, stretching as it travels, then snaps to the new width.
moves.body:
When a tab is selected, the indicator does not jump. It travels from the old tab to the new one, and on the way its leading edge moves ahead of its trailing edge, so it stretches like a drop of liquid and contracts as it lands.

The stretch is what makes the move feel alive. It comes from animating the left and right edges separately, with the edge in the direction of travel moving first.

Use it for:

- Tabs, segmented controls, nav bars
- Filters and category pickers in app demos
- Any time you switch between views in the same screen

Common mistakes:

- Moving the indicator as a rigid box, which looks stiff
- Changing the label colors before the indicator arrives
- Overshooting so much that the pill passes the next tab
- Different durations for short and long jumps that make the motion feel inconsistent

The content below the tabs should switch as the indicator lands, ideally sliding in from the same direction the indicator moved.

moves.name: UI number ticker
moves.summary: A number inside the interface counts or rolls to its new value, digit columns spinning like an odometer, then settles.
moves.body:
A UI number ticker animates a value that lives inside an app screen: a balance, a follower count, a frame counter, a revenue figure. Instead of swapping, the number rolls to its new value so the change is felt.

There are two common styles:

- **Count up**: the value interpolates from start to end with an ease-out, so it races at first and slows near the target
- **Digit roll**: each digit is its own vertical strip that slides to the new digit, like an odometer

It works best when the number is the outcome of something the viewer just watched, such as a click, a send, or data loading.

Common mistakes:

- Proportional fonts, which make the number wobble in width as it changes; use tabular figures
- Linear counting, which hides the landing
- Counting for too long; around one second is usually enough
- Ending on an ugly value, then jumping

Add a small scale bump or color flash on the final digit so the viewer knows the count is finished.

moves.name: Scroll-through screen
moves.summary: A long page or app screen scrolls past inside a frame with eased momentum, stopping on key sections before moving on.
moves.body:
A scroll-through shows more of a page than fits on screen by moving it upward inside a frame, the way a person would scroll. Good scroll motion has momentum: it accelerates, glides, and settles, often with a tiny overshoot back.

The point is not to show every pixel. It is to stop on the sections that matter and move quickly between them.

It works for:

- Landing page and website showcases
- Long app screens like feeds, docs, settings
- Portfolio reels showing several pages

Common mistakes:

- Constant-speed scrolling, which looks like a screen capture of an autoscroll
- Scrolling so fast the text smears and becomes unreadable
- No pauses, so nothing lands
- Scrolling while the frame itself is also moving, which doubles the motion

Treat each scroll as a short move from one stop to the next. A light motion blur on fast segments helps hide stutter, and sections can animate into place as they enter, the way scroll-triggered sites do.

moves.name: Device frame reveal
moves.summary: The shot starts full-screen on the UI, then pulls back as a phone or laptop bezel grows around it, placing the app in a device.
moves.body:
A device frame reveal begins inside the screen. The viewer sees the interface edge to edge, then the frame scales down and a bezel grows outward from the screen edge until a full phone or laptop is visible.

It answers "where does this run?" after the viewer has already seen the UI up close. Running it in reverse, pushing into the screen until the bezel leaves the frame, is a clean way to go from a product shot into the app.

Use it for:

- Mobile app launches
- Switching from detail to context midway through a demo
- Showing the same product on phone and desktop

Common mistakes:

- Letting the screen content shrink as a flat image while the bezel appears separately; they should be one object
- Bezel shapes that do not match a real device's corner radius
- Revealing the device and then moving straight on, with no hold
- Heavy reflections that fight the UI for attention

Add a soft floor shadow as the device appears so it sits in a space rather than floating on a flat color.

moves.name: UI state morph
moves.summary: One shape flows through a chain of interface states, button to loader to check to slider to toast, without ever cutting.
moves.body:
A UI state morph takes a single element and keeps transforming it into the next component. A button squeezes into a loading dot, the dot draws a check, the check stretches into a slider, the slider becomes a toggle. Nothing appears from nowhere; every state is grown from the previous one.

This move works because it is easy to follow. The eye locks onto one object and stays with it for the whole video.

It works for:

- Short beat-synced brand loops
- Showing the breadth of a design system or component library
- Product teasers where the story is a sequence of actions

Common mistakes:

- Crossfading between states instead of reshaping, which breaks the illusion of one object
- Changing too many properties at once; width, height and radius should lead, color and labels follow
- Uneven pacing, so some states feel rushed and others drag
- A loop whose last frame does not match the first

Set each change on a musical beat and let width and corner radius ride springs, so the shape stretches and settles like something soft.

moves.name: Path draw-on
moves.summary: A vector stroke draws itself along its path from start to end, as if an invisible pen were tracing the shape in real time.
moves.body:
A path draw-on reveals a stroke progressively along its own length. In code this is usually a dash pattern the size of the path, with the dash offset animated from full length to zero, or a trimmed path whose end value goes from 0 to 1.

It reads as intent: someone is drawing this right now. That makes it a strong opener for logos, diagrams, signatures, maps and one-line illustrations where the line carries the story from object to object.

Where it works best:

- Line icons and logos before a fill fades in
- Single continuous-line illustrations
- Connectors and arrows in explainers

Common mistakes:

- **Linear speed.** A constant rate looks like a progress bar. Ease the drawn length, and slow down on corners or small details.
- **Ignoring path direction.** If the path was authored right to left, it draws right to left. Reverse it or flip the offset.
- **Drawing everything at once.** Ten strokes finishing together read as a fade. Stagger them, or order them the way a hand would draw.
- **Round caps at length zero** leave a dot on screen before the draw starts. Hide the stroke until progress is above zero.

moves.name: Shape morph
moves.summary: One vector shape smoothly turns into another, its outline flowing from circle to square to whatever comes next without a cut.
moves.body:
A shape morph interpolates the outline of one shape into another. The viewer never sees a swap, only one object changing its mind, so the eye stays locked on a single element through the whole change.

It is the backbone of continuous one-take videos: a dot becomes a button, the button becomes a card, the card becomes a chart. It also works for simple geometry sequences (circle, triangle, square, hexagon) on a beat.

To morph cleanly, both paths need the same number of points in a matching order. Resample both outlines to an equal point count and align their starting points, or use a library that does this for you. For rectangles and pills, animating width, height and corner radius is simpler and cleaner than point interpolation.

Common mistakes:

- **Mismatched start points**, which make the shape twist or turn inside out midway.
- **Morphing too far in one step.** A star into a letter is mush. Pass through an intermediate shape.
- **Even timing.** Give each morph a strong ease-in-out, or a spring with a small overshoot so it settles.
- **Changing color and shape on different curves**, which splits one gesture into two.

moves.name: Vector mask reveal
moves.summary: Content appears through a growing vector shape used as a mask, so the image or scene is revealed in the silhouette of that shape.
moves.body:
In a vector mask reveal, a shape acts as a window. As the shape grows, rotates or slides, it uncovers whatever sits beneath it: a photo, a UI screen, a color field, the next part of the scene.

The shape carries meaning. A circle that grows from a button tells the viewer the button caused the reveal. A mask cut from a logo or product outline ties the reveal to the brand. A plain rectangle wipe has the least character, so pick the shape on purpose.

Good uses:

- Revealing a photo inside a logo letterform or icon
- Growing a circle out of the exact spot a cursor clicked
- Uncovering a product screen through its own rounded-rect frame

Common mistakes:

- **Mask grows from the center of the frame** when the cause sits elsewhere. Anchor it to the origin of the action.
- **Mask stops exactly at the frame edge.** A circle must reach the farthest corner, not the nearest side, or corners stay hidden.
- **Static content under the mask.** Let the revealed layer scale down slightly (around 108% to 100%) as the mask opens so it feels alive.
- **Hard, aliased mask edges** at low resolution.

moves.name: Gooey split and merge
moves.summary: Shapes pull apart and fuse like drops of liquid, stretching a bridge between them before they snap into separate blobs or one.
moves.body:
A gooey split and merge makes separate shapes behave like liquid. When two blobs approach, a neck forms and pulls them together. When one blob divides, it stretches, pinches thin and snaps into two. The effect is usually built with a blur followed by a hard alpha threshold, or with a signed distance field and a smooth union.

It reads as soft, physical and playful. It is ideal when one thing becomes several, or several become one: a pill splitting into three dots, notifications merging into a status bar, a loader dividing into results.

Where it works:

- Dynamic Island style status pills
- Typing indicators and loaders
- Brand marks built from round shapes

Common mistakes:

- **Threshold too low**, which leaves blurry halos instead of crisp liquid edges.
- **Applying the goo to text or icons inside the blobs.** Filter only the blob layer and draw content on top.
- **No squash.** Blobs that move fast should stretch along their direction of travel.
- **Merging at constant speed.** The bridge should snap: slow approach, quick fuse, small wobble after.

moves.name: Trim path loop
moves.summary: A stroke segment chases itself around a path: its head and tail move at different speeds, so the line grows, shrinks and loops forever.
moves.body:
A trim path loop animates both ends of a visible stroke segment instead of drawing the whole path once. The head races ahead while the tail lags, then the tail catches up. Add a slow rotation of the whole path and you get the familiar loading spinner. Run it along a custom path and you get a line that endlessly travels through a logo, a route or a decorative frame.

It reads as ongoing activity. That makes it right for loaders, waiting states, energy flowing through a circuit, or an ambient loop behind a title.

The trick is giving start and end their own easing curves with an offset in time. If both ends move on the same curve, the segment just slides at a fixed length and looks mechanical.

Common mistakes:

- **Seam pops.** On closed paths, the moment the segment wraps past the path's start point can jump. Wrap the values with modulo and test that frame.
- **Segment gets too short** and vanishes into a dot. Keep a minimum length.
- **Loop length that doesn't divide the video.** Make the cycle a whole fraction of the clip so the loop is seamless.

moves.name: Icon morph
moves.summary: A small icon transforms into its next state, like play into pause or menu into close, with its strokes rotating and reshaping in place.
moves.body:
An icon morph changes one glyph into another without a fade. The three bars of a menu rotate into an X. A play triangle splits into two pause bars. A plus spins into a check. Because the icon never disappears, the change feels like a response to the user, not a replacement.

In videos made with code, icon morphs sell product UI: they show that the interface reacts. They are also small, so they belong on a beat or right after a cursor click, not as the main event.

How to build them cleanly:

- Draw both states from the same parts. The X uses the top and bottom menu bars; the middle bar fades or shrinks.
- Rotate parts around a shared center, and keep stroke width and caps identical across states.
- Use 200 to 350 ms for the whole change.

Common mistakes:

- **Crossfading two icons** and calling it a morph.
- **Stroke widths that change** between states, which looks like a bug.
- **Too much overshoot.** A tiny settle is fine; a wobbling icon looks cheap.
- **Rotating the wrong way.** Turn in the direction that matches the action, like clockwise for forward.

moves.name: Geometric pattern build
moves.summary: A geometric pattern assembles step by step from simple primitives, with lines, circles and polygons appearing in a precise construction order.
moves.body:
A geometric pattern build shows how a figure is made. It starts with one primitive, such as a circle or a line, then adds copies, rotations and intersections until a full pattern stands on screen. The order is part of the design: construction lines first, then the shapes they define, then fills and color.

It reads as precise and intelligent. It suits technical brands, math explainers, music visuals and logos built from circles and grids.

What makes it work:

- **One rule repeated.** Rotate by a fixed angle, scale by a fixed ratio, offset by a fixed step.
- **A visible rhythm.** Add one ring or one copy per beat so the build feels musical.
- **Hierarchy of weight.** Thin, faint guides; bolder final shapes. Remove or dim the guides at the end.

Common mistakes:

- Adding pieces in random order, which hides the logic that makes the pattern satisfying.
- Too many elements arriving at once.
- Leaving all construction lines at full strength, so the final figure never resolves.
- Floating point drift in rotated copies, which shows up as hairline gaps. Compute every copy from the original, not from the previous copy.

moves.name: Isometric build
moves.summary: Flat isometric blocks, buildings or devices assemble piece by piece, dropping and extruding into place on a 30-degree grid.
moves.body:
An isometric build animates a scene drawn on an isometric grid, where the three axes sit 120 degrees apart and nothing shrinks with distance. Blocks drop in from above, extrude up from their footprint, or slide along grid axes until a small world is complete: a city, a server stack, a desk, a product diagram.

It reads as a clear, ordered system. Because there is no perspective, every piece stays the same size wherever it sits, so it is easy to explain architectures, pipelines and processes with it.

How to keep it convincing:

- Move pieces only along the three isometric axes or straight down.
- Light it with three fixed face tones (top lightest, one side mid, the other darkest) and keep them consistent.
- Build bottom-up and back-to-front so draw order never breaks.

Common mistakes:

- **Wrong depth sorting.** A block in front drawn before the one behind it. Sort by grid position every frame.
- **Mixing perspective and isometric** elements in one scene.
- **Everything landing at once.** Stagger by 40 to 80 ms and give each landing a small squash.
- **Off-grid positions** that make edges wobble by a pixel.

moves.name: Radial burst
moves.summary: Short lines or shapes shoot outward from a single point in a ring, flaring and fading in a fraction of a second to mark an impact.
moves.body:
A radial burst is a ring of strokes, dots or small shapes that fire outward from one point. Each element travels a short distance, shrinks or trims away, and is gone within a few hundred milliseconds. It is the vector cousin of a spark: a punctuation mark for a moment.

It reads as emphasis. Use it when something lands: a like button, a counter hitting its target, a logo snapping into place. A slower version, with long rays rotating out from a center, works as a logo flourish or a sunburst background.

How to make it feel good:

- Trim the lines from the inside out, so each ray detaches from the center and flies away.
- Use a fast ease-out. Most of the travel happens in the first third.
- Vary length or angle slightly so it doesn't look stamped.

Common mistakes:

- **Too slow.** Above about 500 ms the burst stops being an accent and becomes a distraction.
- **Too many bursts.** Once per scene is plenty; on every beat it becomes wallpaper.
- **Firing from the wrong point.** The burst must come from the exact impact spot.
- Bursts that linger after their moment.

moves.name: Orbiting shapes
moves.summary: Small shapes, icons or words circle a central element on elliptical paths, giving a hub-and-satellites loop that never stops moving.
moves.body:
Orbiting shapes place a central object, such as a logo, a product or a dot, and send smaller elements around it on circular or tilted elliptical paths. Each satellite has its own radius and speed, and the orbits can be drawn as thin lines or left invisible.

It reads as a system with a core: integrations around a product, features around a brand, words around an idea. It also makes a calm, endless loop for backgrounds and end cards.

How to make it read in 2D:

- Squash the orbit vertically (to around 30 to 45% height) so it reads as a tilted ring.
- Scale satellites up and brighten them on the front half, smaller and dimmer on the back half.
- Pass satellites behind the center object on the back half of the ellipse.

Common mistakes:

- **Same speed for every orbit.** Inner orbits should move faster, like real ones.
- **Satellites always in front.** Without depth sorting, the orbit reads as flat circles.
- **Rotating text that becomes upside down.** Keep labels upright while their positions orbit.
- **Loop length mismatched with the video,** so the last frame jumps.

moves.name: Grid tessellation
moves.summary: A surface fills with repeating tiles such as squares, triangles or hexagons that appear, flip or rotate in waves across the grid.
moves.body:
A grid tessellation builds or changes a surface made of identical tiles that fit without gaps. Tiles can pop in one by one, flip to show a new color, rotate to form a different pattern, or grow outward from a single cell into a full honeycomb.

The magic comes from the wave. Each tile runs the same small animation, but its start time depends on its position: distance from a center, a diagonal index, or a noise value. That turns a dull grid into a visible ripple.

Good uses:

- Background textures for titles
- Transitions where tiles flip from one scene to the next
- Building a logo or icon out of cells

Common mistakes:

- **Random order.** Pure random delays look like static. Use a structured wave, with a little noise if needed.
- **Visible seams.** Tiles drawn at fractional positions leave hairline gaps. Overlap each tile by half a pixel or snap to whole pixels.
- **Animating every tile at full contrast** behind text. Keep background grids low contrast.
- **Delays that grow too large.** A wave much longer than the tile animation drags. Aim for the full sweep in under a second.

moves.name: Shard assemble
moves.summary: Faceted polygon shards fly in from around the frame and lock together, one by one, until they form a complete logo or object.
moves.body:
A shard assemble splits a logo or shape into triangles or faceted pieces, scatters them, then flies each piece back to its home position. The pieces may spin, scale and shade as they travel, then snap flush with their neighbors. Often a thin wireframe of the final shape is drawn first, so the viewer sees the target before it fills.

It reads as construction and precision: many parts becoming one thing. It suits tech and gaming logos, crystal styles, and any reveal that should feel built, not shown.

How to make it work:

- Stagger by distance from the center or along one axis so the logo fills in a clear direction.
- Bring pieces in with a strong ease-out, and let them settle with a tiny rotation correction.
- Shade each facet with a slightly different tone so the polygons read.

Common mistakes:

- **Pieces landing at the same moment**, which looks like a crossfade.
- **Visible cracks** in the final logo. On the last frames, swap the shards for the clean vector logo.
- **Pieces flying from random directions** with no pattern, which reads as chaos.
- Running long; 1 to 2 seconds is enough.

moves.name: Particle assemble
moves.summary: Thousands of scattered particles fly in and settle into a logo, word or image, or break apart from it and drift away.
moves.body:
A cloud of points starts loose across the frame, then each point travels to its own target pixel sampled from a logo, word or photo. The shape appears to condense out of dust. Played backwards, the same setup becomes a disintegration.

It reads well because the viewer sees chaos turn into meaning, so it works for logo reveals, title cards and the payoff of a section. It is weaker as background decoration.

- Sample targets from the shape's filled pixels on a grid, then shuffle the order with a seeded random so arrivals do not sweep in reading order.
- Give each particle a slightly different start time and duration. All of them landing on the same frame looks mechanical.
- Ease the final 20 percent hard so the shape locks into crisp edges, then cross to the real vector logo once the dots are settled.

**Common mistakes:** too few particles (the shape never reads), particles still jittering after they land, and using `Math.random()` per frame so every render differs. Compute every position from the frame number and a seed.

moves.name: Flow field
moves.summary: Particles drift along an invisible current defined by noise, leaving soft streaks that look like wind, smoke or iron filings.
moves.body:
A flow field assigns a direction to every point in the frame, usually from 2D or 3D noise. Particles read that direction each step and move along it, so thousands of points follow coherent, swirling lanes instead of random paths. Draw their recent positions as thin lines and the field becomes visible as streams.

It works as a living background behind type, as a texture for abstract openers, and as a metaphor for data, traffic or ideas moving.

- Use curl noise or rotate gradient noise 90 degrees so particles circulate instead of piling into sinks.
- Keep the noise scale large: two or three big swirls across the frame read better than dozens of small eddies.
- Animate the field itself slowly through a third noise dimension so the currents evolve.

**Common mistakes:** simulating step by step in a way that breaks when the renderer jumps to frame 400, trails that fill the screen to a gray mush, and contrast high enough to fight the text on top. Precompute paths deterministically or integrate from frame zero with a fixed step.

moves.name: Noise displacement
moves.summary: Coherent noise pushes vertices or pixels around over time, so a flat shape, grid or surface ripples and breathes like something alive.
moves.body:
Displacement offsets each vertex or pixel by a value sampled from smooth noise. Move through the noise over time and the surface undulates: a plane becomes rolling terrain, a sphere becomes a blob, a line becomes a hand-drawn wobble, a photo warps like heat haze.

It is the base ingredient of most organic looks in code-made video. Use it to make rigid geometry feel soft, to give a still frame life during a long hold, or to transition between states by ramping the amount up and back down.

- Layer two octaves: one large slow wave for the overall shape and one small faster one for surface detail at about a quarter of the strength.
- Animate the amplitude, not just the time offset. A ramp from 0 to full and back is a ready-made transition.
- Keep motion speed low. Noise that changes fast reads as jitter, not as life.

**Common mistakes:** displacing text you want people to read, using white noise instead of gradient noise, and a seed that changes between renders.

moves.name: Instanced grid
moves.summary: A large grid of identical dots, tiles or cubes where every cell reacts to one shared field, producing ripples, waves and shapes that sweep across.
moves.body:
One shape repeated hundreds or thousands of times in rows and columns, with each copy's scale, height, color or rotation driven by a single function of its position and time. A distance-from-center sine gives a ripple, a moving point gives a wake, a sampled image turns the grid into a low-resolution picture.

The grid reads as one organism, which makes it good for tech and data themes, for transitions where a pixel image resolves out of the field, and for loops.

- Drive everything from one field function, for example `sin(distance * k - t * speed)`, and map it to two properties at once, such as scale and brightness.
- Add a small per-cell delay from distance so motion visibly travels instead of happening everywhere at once.
- Use real instancing (WebGL, Three.js `InstancedMesh`) above a few thousand cells; separate DOM nodes will crawl.

**Common mistakes:** cells so small the pattern turns to moire after video compression, perfectly uniform motion with no falloff, and a grid that never resolves into anything meaningful.

moves.name: L-system growth
moves.summary: Lines branch and split from a single seed point into a tree, root network or vein pattern that grows across the frame over time.
moves.body:
Growth systems start from one point and repeatedly split into branches according to rules: an L-system rewrites a string of turtle commands, recursion splits each branch into two shorter ones at an angle, and space colonization grows toward scattered attractor points. Animated, the structure creeps outward generation by generation.

It reads as growth, connection and spreading, so it fits stories about networks, ecosystems, teams, roots of an idea or a product reaching more people.

- Generate the full structure once with a seed, store each segment with its depth, then reveal segments by depth over time. Rendering stays a pure function of the frame.
- Taper stroke width by depth and slightly vary angles with the seed so it looks grown, not drawn with a ruler.
- Let children start before parents finish, overlapping by about half a segment, so growth flows instead of stepping.

**Common mistakes:** perfectly symmetric trees that look like clip art, too many generations so the tips become noise, and growth at a constant speed with no slowdown at the tips.

moves.name: Flocking boids
moves.summary: Many small agents steer by three simple rules, separation, alignment and cohesion, so they move together like a flock of birds or a school of fish.
moves.body:
Each agent looks at its neighbors and adjusts its heading to avoid crowding, match their direction and stay near the group. No one leads, yet the whole swarm turns, splits and rejoins like a living thing.

It reads as collective behavior: communities, crowds, markets, many users acting together. A target force lets the flock gather into a shape or chase a point, which turns ambient motion into storytelling.

- Tune separation radius first. It sets the density of the flock more than any other value.
- Cap speed and turn rate so agents bank smoothly instead of snapping.
- Point each agent along its velocity. Orientation is what sells the effect, even with simple triangles.
- Simulate from frame zero with a fixed timestep and seeded start positions, or bake the paths to a buffer, so any frame renders the same.

**Common mistakes:** too few agents to look like a group, all agents at the same speed, a flock that stays clumped in the middle of the frame forever, and simulation tied to real time so the render differs from the preview.

moves.name: Voronoi cells
moves.summary: The frame splits into organic cells around moving seed points, with borders that shift and redraw as the points drift, like foam, cracked mud or stained glass.
moves.body:
A Voronoi diagram divides space so each region contains every pixel closest to one seed point. Animate the points and the borders slide, cells grow and shrink, and neighbors trade edges. The look sits between biology and architecture: skin cells, giraffe patches, dried earth, stained glass.

It works for themes of territory, partitioning and many parts making a whole, and as a shattered-glass transition when cells fly apart.

- Move seeds slowly with seeded noise. Fast seeds make borders flicker.
- Use Lloyd relaxation once at setup for even cell sizes, or leave it off for a rougher, more natural look.
- Fill cells from a short palette and keep borders thin and consistent. The pattern does the work.
- For a shatter, give each cell its own spin and drift outward from the impact point with a short stagger by distance.

**Common mistakes:** hundreds of tiny cells that turn to noise on a phone, rainbow fills, and recomputing the diagram with a library that returns cells in different order each frame, which makes colors jump.

moves.name: Reaction-diffusion
moves.summary: Two simulated chemicals spread and react to grow labyrinths, spots and coral-like stripes that slowly fill the frame from a seed.
moves.body:
Reaction-diffusion simulates two substances that diffuse at different rates and convert each other. Depending on two rates (feed and kill), the result settles into spots, stripes, mazes or splitting cells. The growth front creeps outward and fills shapes in a way that feels biological rather than drawn.

Use it when something should feel alive or grown: a logo filling with coral texture, a background that evolves over a whole film, a transition where pattern spreads to cover the frame.
