- Seed inside a mask, such as a logo or word, and confine growth to it for a strong reveal.
- Run thousands of simulation steps per second of video. Render several steps per frame on the GPU.
- Map the concentration through a two-color ramp with a sharp threshold. Smooth gradients look muddy.

**Common mistakes:** parameters that die out to blank or explode to noise, running in real time so renders vary, and starting from random noise everywhere instead of a deliberate seed. Simulate once with a fixed step count per frame and cache frames if the renderer seeks.

moves.name: Metaballs
moves.summary: Soft round blobs drift and, when close, stretch and fuse into one gooey surface, then neck and split apart again like a lava lamp.
moves.body:
Each blob contributes a falloff field. Summing the fields and drawing everything above a threshold gives a surface where nearby blobs merge with smooth necks instead of overlapping as hard circles. Pull them apart and the neck thins and snaps.

It reads as liquid, playful and cohesive, good for merging ideas, joining teams, loading states and transitions where one shape splits into many or many pool into one.

- In 2D, the cheapest version is blur plus a contrast threshold (an SVG `feColorMatrix` alpha clamp or a shader step). In 3D, raymarch a smooth-minimum distance field.
- Keep blob sizes varied, roughly 1x to 2.5x between smallest and largest.
- Time merges so the neck forms over 8 to 12 frames. Faster and it pops, slower and it looks stuck.

**Common mistakes:** blurry edges because the threshold is too soft, blobs that never touch so the effect never shows, and running the blur on large full-frame layers that slow renders to a crawl.

moves.name: Ordered dither
moves.summary: Images, gradients or 3D renders reduced to a small set of colors through a fixed threshold pattern, giving a crisp 1-bit, retro-print look.
moves.body:
Ordered dithering compares each pixel against a small repeating threshold matrix, usually a 4x4 or 8x8 Bayer pattern, and outputs one of two (or a few) colors. Gradients become cross-hatched textures and 3D shading becomes a lattice of dots. Because the matrix is fixed, the pattern stays put while the image under it moves, which looks intentional rather than noisy.

It suits tech, retro computing and editorial looks, and it makes generic 3D or gradients feel designed.

- Quantize at a coarse pixel size (3 to 6 screen pixels per dither cell) and upscale with nearest-neighbor so it survives video compression.
- Pick two colors with strong contrast from the brand palette, not just black and white.
- Keep the matrix fixed in screen space. Re-randomizing per frame turns it into static.

**Common mistakes:** dither cells so fine that the encoder smears them into gray, applying it over small text, and using error diffusion (Floyd-Steinberg) on moving footage, which crawls and shimmers from frame to frame.

moves.name: Attractor trails
moves.summary: Points follow the equations of a strange attractor, tracing glowing ribbons that loop around invisible centers without ever repeating.
moves.body:
A strange attractor is a small set of equations, such as Lorenz, Aizawa, Thomas or Clifford, whose solutions orbit forever without settling or repeating. Integrate thousands of points through it and draw their recent history, and you get dense, woven ribbon forms that slowly rotate in 3D.

It reads as complexity with order inside, so it suits science, AI, finance and anything about systems or chaos. It also makes a striking slow backdrop for a single line of type.

- Integrate with a small fixed step from seeded starting points, and precompute positions so any frame can be rendered directly.
- Color by speed or by the age of the trail segment. A gradient along the trail shows direction.
- Rotate the camera slowly around the form. Most attractors only make sense in three dimensions.

**Common mistakes:** a single trail that looks like a scribble, step sizes so large the shape breaks down, and additive glow cranked up until the core is a white blob with no structure.

moves.name: Infinite fractal zoom
moves.summary: The camera dives into a self-similar shape forever: every level reveals the same pattern again, so the zoom loops seamlessly.
moves.body:
A self-similar structure, either a true fractal like the Mandelbrot set or a designed recursion where a shape contains a smaller copy of itself, lets the camera zoom without end. When the zoom reaches the next copy at exactly the scale of the start, the loop point is invisible.

It reads as depth, infinity and detail inside detail, good for loops, intros and ideas like scale, recursion or a product that contains whole worlds.

- Zoom on a log scale: scale = `base ^ t`, not a linear ramp. Linear zoom looks like it accelerates forever.
- For a designed recursion, place the child copy at a fixed ratio (for example 1/8) and offset, then loop when scale reaches 8x.
- For true fractals, use double precision or perturbation once zoom passes about 10^6, or the image dissolves into blocks.

**Common mistakes:** a zoom target that drifts off the detail so the screen fills with flat color, a visible jump at the loop point, and too much rotation stacked on the zoom.

moves.name: Dolly in
moves.summary: The whole frame moves steadily closer to the subject, so attention narrows onto one thing without a cut.
moves.body:
A dolly in moves the camera toward the subject over one to three seconds. In a code-made video the "camera" is usually one transform on a world container, so a dolly in is a scale and translate on that container, not on each element.

It reads as "look here, this matters." Use it to go from a full layout to the one button, number or line that the scene is about.

- Push **1.1x to 1.3x** over 1.2 to 2.5 s. Bigger pushes start to feel like a zoom effect, not a camera.
- Interpolate scale in log space. Linear scale looks like it speeds up toward the end.
- Keep captions, logo bug and grain outside the world so they do not grow with it.

Common mistakes: pushing while text is still typing and reflowing, pushing into a screenshot past its native resolution so it goes soft, and following a push straight away with a pull out, which reads as indecision. End the move with a settle, never a hard stop.

moves.name: Breathing push
moves.summary: A barely visible, continuous push of 2 to 4 percent during a hold that keeps a static frame feeling alive.
moves.body:
A breathing push is a camera move the viewer should not consciously notice. During a hold, the world scales from 1.00 to about 1.03 across the whole shot, so a still frame never looks frozen.

It works on title cards, quotes, end cards, product hero shots and any moment where the content is done animating but the frame needs to stay on screen for reading time.

- Keep it between **2 and 4 percent** of scale for the full hold, 2 to 6 seconds.
- Use linear or a very soft ease. It should feel like drift, not a move.
- When the next scene starts, begin it at the scale where this one ended, or reset on a cut.

Common mistakes: pushing hard enough that it becomes a dolly in, applying it to text layers that then shimmer as they resample, and stacking it with other camera moves in the same shot. If the renderer shows subpixel jitter, render text outside the world or at a higher scale.

moves.name: Punch in
moves.summary: A sudden 4 to 8 frame jump in framing, tighter on the subject, used to hit a beat or a key word.
moves.body:
A punch in is a fast, short reframe: the camera snaps closer in a handful of frames and then holds. It comes from editing, where a punch in is a crop on the same take, and in code it plays the same role: emphasis without a new shot.

Use it on a music hit, the landing of an object, or the word in a line that carries the meaning. Small values work best. A **4 to 15 percent** punch already reads clearly; larger values belong to a crash zoom.

- Spend 4 to 8 frames on the move, then hold.
- Use a snappy ease-out or a stiff spring with almost no overshoot.
- Release with a slower move or on the next cut, never as a mirror of the punch.

Common mistakes: punching on every beat until it reads as a twitch, punching into soft or low-resolution assets, and timing the punch a frame after the sound. Land the move on the hit frame or one frame before it.

moves.name: Crash zoom
moves.summary: A violent, very fast zoom from wide to tight with motion blur, used for comedy, shock or a hard reveal.
moves.body:
A crash zoom rushes the camera from a wide frame to a tight one in under half a second, usually with heavy motion blur and sometimes a slight overshoot. It is louder than a punch in: the travel itself is the point.

It works for reveals ("and the winner is..."), comic double takes, and energetic social edits where a moment needs a jolt. Use it once or twice per film at most.

- Go from 1x to **2x or more** in 6 to 12 frames.
- Ease in hard and stop hard: an expo-in curve, a short settle, then hold.
- Add radial or directional blur only during the fastest frames.

Common mistakes: zooming linearly, which looks like a slideshow transition; landing off target so the subject drifts into frame after the move; and zooming into a raster image that turns to mush at 3x. If the subject is a screenshot, build it big or vector so the end frame is sharp.

moves.name: Pull back reveal
moves.summary: The camera pulls away from a detail to show the larger scene it belongs to, turning a close-up into context.
moves.body:
A pull back reveal starts tight on one element and moves the camera away until the surrounding scene explains it: a single bubble becomes a chat inside a phone, a button becomes a full dashboard, a word becomes a sentence.

It is the natural closer for a sequence. Close-ups set up "what is this," the pull back answers "this is where it lives."

- Pull from about **1.3x to 1.0x** (or further for big reveals) over 1.5 to 3 s.
- Interpolate in log scale so the pace feels even as the frame widens.
- Let new elements arrive during the pull so the wider frame is not empty.

Common mistakes: revealing context that was never designed (empty edges, cut-off UI), pulling back and then immediately pushing in again, and starting the pull while the close-up text is still being read. If the reveal is very large, like a desktop shrinking to a dot, split it into eased segments with short holds rather than one long linear drift.

moves.name: Parallax layers
moves.summary: Foreground, midground and background move at different speeds as the camera travels, creating depth from flat layers.
moves.body:
Parallax fakes depth by moving each layer by an amount inversely related to its distance. Near layers slide far, distant layers barely move. It is the oldest trick in the multiplane camera and still the cheapest way to make a flat scene feel spatial.

It works for title scenes, illustrated explainers, product shots over a backdrop and slow lateral camera moves.

- Use 3 to 5 depth planes. Typical speed ratios: background 0.2, midground 0.5, subject 1.0, foreground 1.4.
- Make distant layers smaller, slightly blurred (2 to 8 px) and shifted 10 to 30 percent toward the background color.
- Drive every layer from one camera value so the ratios stay locked.

Common mistakes: animating each layer with its own keyframes, so the depth drifts apart; foreground layers that move fast across text and hurt readability; and gaps at the edges of slower layers. Oversize every layer by its maximum travel so no edge ever shows.

moves.name: Camera orbit
moves.summary: The camera circles around a subject on an arc, revealing its sides and depth while keeping it centered.
moves.body:
An orbit moves the camera along an arc around a subject while always looking at it. The subject stays put in the center; the world and lighting swing around it. It reads as inspection and gives a product or a 3D object weight.

It works in real 3D scenes and in 2.5D setups where a card, device or logo can rotate on its Y axis with perspective.

- A partial arc is usually stronger than a full turn: **10 to 40 degrees** over 3 to 8 seconds.
- Keep the speed even in the middle and ease only at the ends, or loop with constant speed.
- Combine with a small push (10 to 25 percent) only if it is designed as one arc.

Common mistakes: orbiting a flat element far enough that it goes edge-on and disappears, letting text in the scene rotate into unreadable angles, and orbiting at a rate that strobes on fine detail. With 2.5D cards, keep perspective between 1200 and 2000 px so the distortion stays believable.

moves.name: Rack focus
moves.summary: Focus shifts from one layer to another: the old subject softens into blur while the new one sharpens.
moves.body:
A rack focus moves attention between two subjects at different depths without moving the camera. One layer blurs out while the other comes into focus, so the viewer's eye follows the sharp area.

In code it is an animated blur on two or more layers, sometimes with a small scale change to mimic focus breathing on a real lens.

- Defocused layers sit at **6 to 12 px** of blur; the focused one at 0.
- Transfer over 0.5 to 0.8 seconds with a smooth move curve.
- Start the incoming sharpen a few frames after the outgoing blur begins.

It works for over-the-shoulder setups, a phone in the foreground with a dashboard behind it, or a headline in front of an image. Use it once or twice per film; it is a strong signal.

Common mistakes: blurring text that still needs to be read, animating heavy blur in a renderer that cannot keep up (pre-render the layers if needed), and racking between layers that sit at the same apparent depth, which just looks like a fade.

moves.name: Camera shake
moves.summary: The frame jitters with decaying, seeded noise for a few frames after an impact, or drifts gently like a handheld camera.
moves.body:
Camera shake comes in two flavors. **Impact shake** is a short, decaying jolt on a hit: a slam, a drop, a bass hit. **Handheld drift** is a slow, low-amplitude wander that makes a shot feel filmed rather than generated.

Both should be driven by seeded noise, not random numbers per frame, so renders are repeatable and the motion is smooth enough to read as a camera.

- Impact: 2 to 6 px of translation (plus up to 0.5 degrees of rotation), 3 to 6 frames, decaying to zero.
- Handheld: 1 to 3 px, noise frequency around 0.5 to 1.5 Hz, continuous.
- Shake the world container, not the captions.

Common mistakes: shaking text that must be read, using white noise that looks like a broken render, shaking every hit until nothing feels like an impact, and shaking in calm UI documentation where it reads as a bug. Many polished brand films ban it outright; keep it for energetic or physical moments.

moves.name: Dolly zoom
moves.summary: The subject holds its size while the background stretches or compresses behind it, creating an uneasy shift in space.
moves.body:
A dolly zoom moves the camera toward or away from the subject while changing the field of view in the opposite direction. The subject stays the same size on screen, but the background seems to rush away or close in. It reads as realization, dread or a sudden shift in perspective.

In 3D, animate camera distance and FOV together so `distance × tan(fov / 2)` stays constant. In 2.5D, keep the subject layer at a fixed scale while background layers scale at different rates by depth.

- A strong effect needs a real depth gap and a background with lines or texture.
- Run it slow (2 to 4 s) for unease, fast (under 1 s) for a jolt or a riser.

Common mistakes: a flat background with nothing to show the stretch, letting the subject drift in size because the math is not locked, and using it as a generic transition. It is a statement move: once per film is plenty.

moves.name: 2.5D camera projection
moves.summary: A still image is split into depth layers or mapped onto depth, so a virtual camera can move through it with real parallax.
moves.body:
2.5D camera projection turns a flat picture into a shallow 3D set. The image is cut into layers (subject, mid, background) or paired with a depth map, and a virtual camera moves a short distance through it. Near parts shift more than far parts, so a photo or illustration gains real volume.

It works for archival photos, AI-generated stills, illustrated backgrounds and establishing shots where you have no footage.

- Keep camera travel small: a slow push or lateral drift of **3 to 8 percent** of the frame.
- Fill the holes behind cut-out subjects (inpaint or extend the background) before moving.
- Add a little focus blur on far layers to sell the depth.

Common mistakes: moving too far so stretched pixels and torn edges appear around the subject, using a noisy depth map that wobbles hair and fine detail, and combining it with a fast orbit. Short, slow moves are the whole trick.

moves.name: Overhead fly-over
moves.summary: The camera glides low over a surface, then rises to a straight-down overhead view that shows the whole layout at once.
moves.body:
A fly-over treats a flat thing, like a landing page, a map, a board or a desk of objects, as a landscape. The camera starts low and tilted, glides across it, then cranes up to look straight down so the whole layout reads as one picture.

It is a strong single-take move for showing something long: a page, a timeline, a workflow. The low pass gives scale and detail, the overhead gives structure.

- Fly the low pass at one steady speed; ease only at the start.
- Rise in log scale with a slow-down into the overhead and a short hold there.
- Use shallow depth of field on the low pass so near content softens.

Common mistakes: changing speed constantly so it feels like a drone in wind, tilting so steeply the content becomes unreadable, and rising past the point where text is legible without holding long enough to show the full layout. Keep one continuous camera; a cut in the middle breaks the effect.

moves.name: Film grain
moves.summary: A fine layer of monochrome noise, regenerated every frame, that makes flat vector or UI frames feel shot rather than exported.
moves.body:
Film grain is a thin layer of random luminance noise laid over the frame and refreshed on every frame. It makes clean vector work read as a physical image, and it covers the banding that 8-bit encoders put into large soft gradients.

It works best on flat color fields, dark scenes and long gradients, and on films that want a warm, slightly analog feel. It is wrong for UI documentation where every pixel of the product should be sharp.

- Keep it small: about **1.5 to 4 percent** luminance, monochrome, not colored speckle.
- Regenerate it each frame (or every second frame for a slower, filmic pulse). A frozen grain pattern looks like a dirty screen.
- Seed the generator from the frame number so renders are identical every time.
- Put it above the world and below the text, or above everything at lower strength.

Common mistakes: grain so heavy it eats small type, grain that only covers one layer so its edge shows, and grain that disappears after encoding because it was too fine for the bitrate. Check the final MP4, not the preview.

moves.name: Chromatic aberration
moves.summary: Red and blue channels drift a pixel or two apart toward the frame edges, giving a lens-like color fringe on high-contrast shapes.
moves.body:
Chromatic aberration imitates a cheap or wide lens: the red, green and blue channels land in slightly different places, so hard edges pick up a thin warm fringe on one side and a cool fringe on the other. Done lightly, it makes a computer-made frame feel like it passed through glass.

It works on high-contrast edges, hand-drawn or retro looks, and as a brief accent on an impact frame. Real lenses fringe more at the edges than in the center, so the offset should grow with distance from the frame center.

- Keep the resting offset at **1 to 2 px** at 1080p, near zero in the center.
- Shift channels outward from center (radial), not all in one direction.
- Clamp at the frame edge so a colored border does not appear.
- Spike it briefly (3 to 6 frames) on a hit, then settle back.

Common mistakes: a constant 6 px split over everything, which reads as a broken monitor, and fringing on small body text, which makes it unreadable. If the viewer notices the effect before the content, it is too strong.

moves.name: Halftone
moves.summary: Tone is drawn as a grid of dots whose size follows brightness, giving a printed, comic-book or newspaper finish that can animate.
moves.body:
Halftone turns a continuous image into a grid of dots: dark areas get big dots, light areas get small ones. In motion it does two jobs. It is a finish that makes photos and gradients look printed, and it is a graphic element in its own right, a field of dots that can grow, flip color or sweep across the frame as a transition.

It suits editorial, comic, manga and poster styles, and explainer graphics that want a print feel without image assets.

- Pick a cell size you can see on a phone: around **8 to 16 px** at 1080p.
- Rotate the grid (15 or 45 degrees) for a classic print look.
- Animate dot radius from a value (brightness, a gradient, a moving falloff) rather than moving the grid itself.
- Keep text out of the halftone or on a solid plate above it.

Common mistakes: cells so small they turn into moire or mush after compression, a grid that slides with the camera and flickers, and halftone applied to everything so nothing stands out.

moves.name: Glow and bloom
moves.summary: Bright parts of the frame bleed a soft halo of light into their surroundings, so the lead element looks lit rather than drawn.
moves.body:
Bloom takes the brightest pixels in a frame, blurs them, and adds them back on top, so light spills past edges the way it does in a camera. A glow is the same idea on one element: a blurred copy behind it. Used on one thing, it tells the viewer where the light is and where to look.

It works on dark backgrounds, neon and screen-light looks, emissive 3D materials, and a hero card that needs to separate from its background.

- One light source per scene, on the lead only.
- Threshold the bloom so only the brightest 5 to 10 percent of pixels contribute.
- Keep glow opacity low (**15 to 35 percent**) and the radius wide and soft.
- Fade the glow in after the element lands, over 300 to 500 ms.

Common mistakes: glow on every icon and label, which looks like a default effect, and bloom on white text that blurs the letterforms. Bright things on dark backgrounds already look bigger, so a strong glow makes them look swollen.

moves.name: Paper texture
moves.summary: A visible paper surface with fibers and tooth sits under the artwork, and ink or color sits in it, so the film reads as made by hand.
moves.body:
Paper texture puts a physical surface under the animation: a warm off-white with faint fibers, tooth and uneven tone. Strokes and fills then pick up that surface, getting lighter where the paper is raised. The result reads as drawn, printed or cut by hand, even when everything is generated in code.

It suits hand-drawn, crayon, pencil, collage and storybook styles, and explainers that want warmth instead of a software look.

- Generate the texture from low-frequency noise for tone plus high-frequency noise for tooth, or use one scanned sheet.
- Multiply the artwork onto the paper so the texture shows through the color.
- Keep the paper still. If the camera moves, the paper moves with the scene, not in screen space.
- Add a very slight per-frame jitter (boil) to line work only if the style is frame-by-frame.

Common mistakes: a tiled texture with a visible repeat, paper that is too dark so contrast drops, and crisp vector UI pasted on top, which breaks the illusion.

moves.name: CRT scanlines
moves.summary: Thin dark horizontal lines, a slight screen curve and a soft phosphor glow make the frame look like it is playing on an old tube monitor.
moves.body:
The CRT look recreates an old tube screen: dark horizontal scanlines, a faint bulge toward the corners, a vignette, a little glow around bright pixels and sometimes a slow brightness roll. It sets a time period instantly and gives retro-futuristic films a strong identity.

Use it for retro or archival sequences, terminal and hacker aesthetics, and footage that is meant to be shown on a screen inside the scene. It can be the whole film's finish or only the content of one TV in the frame.

- Scanline period of **3 to 4 px** at 1080p, darkening 15 to 30 percent.
- Add a slow rolling band (a brighter stripe moving down every 4 to 8 seconds) rather than constant flicker.
- Barrel distortion should be small, a few percent at the corners.
- Pair with a soft glow and a 1 px channel offset.

Common mistakes: scanlines too fine for the output size, which turn into moire after scaling, fast flicker that can hurt viewers, and a CRT finish on the end card where the logo must be clean.

moves.name: Mesh gradient
moves.summary: Several soft color points drift slowly under a background, blending into a smooth, shifting field of color that never quite repeats.
moves.body:
A mesh gradient blends color from several control points instead of a single line, so the background looks like soft, flowing light. Animated, the points drift on slow paths and the colors pool and separate. It gives a scene depth and movement without adding objects.

It works as a background behind product shots, hero type and glass UI, and as a brand color field on title cards. It depends on the palette: three to five colors from the brand, close in value, read as calm. Saturated opposites read as noise.

- Use 3 to 5 points, each moving on a slow loop (**8 to 20 seconds** per cycle).
- Interpolate in OKLab or OKLCH so blends do not go gray.
- Add 1 to 3 percent grain on top to stop banding in the encode.
- Keep motion slow enough that the eye stays on the foreground.

Common mistakes: the generic purple-blue gradient orb, which reads as template design, motion fast enough to compete with the content, and a perfectly smooth gradient that bands into stripes once compressed.

moves.name: Risograph print
moves.summary: Two or three flat spot-color inks overlap with grainy fills and a slight misregistration, like a small-run risograph poster.
moves.body:
The risograph look comes from cheap stencil printing: a few flat spot inks, visible grain inside fills, overlaps that create a third color, and layers that do not quite line up. It reads as indie, editorial and human, and it is a strong way to give a whole film one coherent finish.

It suits studio intros, posters that move, event promos and explainers with a zine feel. Duotone, mapping an image to two inks, is the simplest version.

- Limit the palette to **2 or 3 inks** plus paper. Overlaps multiply.
- Offset one ink layer by **2 to 4 px**, and change the offset only on hits, not every frame.
- Fill shapes with stipple or grain rather than flat color.
- Keep small text in one ink so it stays readable.

Common mistakes: misregistration that jitters on every frame, which looks like a rendering bug, too many colors so the print logic is lost, and photos dropped in at full color next to riso graphics.

moves.name: Light sweep
moves.summary: A narrow band of light slides across a logo, card or button once, as if it caught a reflection, then the surface settles back.
moves.body:
A light sweep is a soft, angled highlight that travels across a surface once. It suggests the object is glossy and physical, and it marks a moment: the logo is done, the card is ready, the product has arrived.

It works as a lockup move on end cards, on metallic or glass surfaces, and on a hero button or badge after it lands. It is a full stop, so it belongs at the end of a phrase.

- Run it **once per film**, or once per hero object, over **600 to 1000 ms** on the film's main ease.
- Angle the band 20 to 30 degrees from vertical; make it 10 to 20 percent of the object's width.
- Clip it to the object's shape and use an additive or screen blend at low opacity.
- Start it after the object has fully settled.

Common mistakes: repeating the sweep on a loop, which turns it into a loading shimmer, a band so bright it washes out the logo, and a sweep over a matte, flat design where no light could reflect.

moves.name: Motion blur
moves.summary: Fast-moving elements smear along their path within each frame, the way a camera shutter records them, so quick moves look smooth instead of strobing.
moves.body:
A real camera keeps its shutter open for part of each frame, so anything moving quickly smears along its path. Rendered frames are instants, so fast motion in code looks choppy and strobes. Motion blur adds the smear back, and it is often the single biggest difference between a cheap and a finished-looking render.

Use it on fast moves: whips, pushes, flying cards, spinning shapes, quick slides. Elements at rest should be perfectly sharp.

- **Subframe accumulation** is the most faithful: render several moments inside each frame and average them. Four subframes cover moderate speed; very fast moves need eight or more.
- A 180-degree shutter (samples spread over half the frame) is a natural default.
- Cheaper option: blur each element along its direction of travel, scaled by speed, zero when settled.
- Never average across a cut.

Common mistakes: visible ghost copies from too few subframes, blur on text that has stopped, and blur that points in a different direction from the motion.

moves.name: Ink bleed
moves.summary: Ink or paint spreads from a point into the paper with ragged, feathered edges, revealing an image or shape the way wet media soaks in.
moves.body:
Ink bleed imitates wet media soaking into paper. A mark starts as a drop and spreads outward with an uneven, fibrous edge, darker where the ink pools and lighter at the fringe. It can be a texture on strokes or a reveal: the next image appears inside a growing ink stain.

It suits ink painting and watercolor styles, hand-made explainers, title reveals over paper and quiet, contemplative films.

- Grow the mask from a seed point with noise on its edge so the boundary is ragged, not circular.
- Spread fast at first and slow down (ease out over **800 to 1500 ms**), like real absorption.
- Darken the edge slightly where pigment collects.
- Let the paper texture show through the ink.

Common mistakes: a perfectly round expanding circle with a blur on it, which reads as a vector mask, spreading at constant speed, and ink that bleeds over clean UI or small type. Wet media looks best when it stays on paper.

moves.name: Grainy gradient
moves.summary: A soft color gradient carries visible noise so it looks tactile and printed, and so it survives video compression without banding.
moves.body:
A grainy gradient is a smooth color ramp with noise mixed into it. The noise does two things. It gives the gradient a tactile, almost sprayed surface instead of a plastic one, and it breaks up the flat steps that 8-bit video turns large gradients into.

It works for backgrounds, glow shapes behind type, sky-like fields and any large area of soft color, especially in dark films where banding is worst.

- Add noise **before** quantizing to 8 bits, at about 1 to 3 percent for invisible dithering or 5 to 10 percent for a visible grainy style.
- Use monochrome noise so hue stays stable.
- Animate the noise per frame for a living surface, or keep it fixed if the gradient itself moves.
- Check the gradient in the final encode at the target bitrate.

Common mistakes: adding grain only to the preview and losing it in export, noise so strong it competes with the content, and high-contrast gradients where no amount of noise hides the steps.

moves.name: Bar chart race
moves.summary: Horizontal bars grow and swap rank over time while a large date counter ticks, showing who leads and when the lead changes.
moves.body:
A bar chart race plays a ranking through time. Each row is a bar with a label and value; as the clock advances, bars stretch or shrink and slide past each other when their rank changes. A big date or year in a corner tells the viewer where they are.

It works when the story is about **overtakes**: market share, popularity, records. It fails when the order barely changes, because then it is just a slow bar chart.

What makes it readable:

- Interpolate values between data points every frame, and animate rank position separately with a short ease so swaps glide instead of teleporting.
- Keep the axis scale moving smoothly toward the current maximum, never jumping.
- Show 8 to 12 bars. More turns into noise.
- Give each entity a fixed color for the whole run.

Common mistakes: linear rank swaps that cross bars through each other with no easing, labels that jitter because numerals are not tabular, and a pace so fast that no overtake can be read. Slow down around the moments that matter.

moves.name: Line chart draw-on
moves.summary: A chart line draws itself from left to right with a glowing head, so the viewer follows the trend as it happens instead of seeing it all at once.
moves.body:
The line is revealed along its length, usually by animating the stroke dash offset or clipping the path from left to right. A small dot or glow rides the leading tip, and the latest value can travel with it as a label.

Use it when the shape of the trend is the message: growth, a crash, a recovery. The draw speed sets the drama, so let it slow down near the key turn and arrive at the final point with a gentle ease.

Things that help:

- Draw the axis and gridlines first, faint, so the line has a stage.
- Fill the area under the line a beat later with a low-opacity gradient.
- End with a small pulse or callout on the last point.

Common mistakes: drawing at constant speed over an uneven path, which makes steep segments feel rushed; letting the camera or axis rescale while the line draws; and smoothing the data so much that real dips disappear. A wobbly, decorative line reads as fake; the line should be the data.

moves.name: Counter roll-up
moves.summary: A big number counts up from zero and decelerates onto its final value, often with a small punch when it lands.
moves.body:
The counter roll-up turns a single statistic into an event. The number climbs quickly at first, then slows as it approaches the target, and lands with a tiny scale bump, a color change or a sound hit.

It works for one strong number per shot: users, revenue, time saved. Two counters running at once split attention, so stagger them or pick one.

Details that matter:

- Use **tabular numerals** and reserve the final width so the digits do not jitter or re-center.
- Ease the value, not the frame rate: an ease-out curve on the value gives the deceleration for free.
- Round to display precision every frame and format with separators (1,240,000 rather than 1240000).
- Pair the number with its unit and a short label in the same block.

Common mistakes: linear counting that stops abruptly, counting so long the viewer stops caring (under 1.5 seconds is usually enough), and fake precision like decimals that flicker. Only animate real numbers.

moves.name: Donut chart sweep
moves.summary: Donut or pie segments sweep around the circle one after another, each settling into its share while the percentage counts beside it.
moves.body:
A donut sweep builds a part-to-whole chart by growing each segment's arc around the ring. Segments start from 12 o'clock and fill clockwise in order, so the eye reads the shares as they arrive.

It suits proportions with few parts: two to five segments. A single-value version (one arc on a faint track) is the cleanest way to show a percentage like 72%.

What makes it read well:

- Sweep each segment with an ease-out, and start the next one just before the previous one finishes so it feels continuous.
- Leave a small gap between segments, and round the stroke caps only if there are very few of them.
- Put the key number in the hole and count it in sync with the sweep.
- Pull the important segment out slightly or brighten it after the build.

Common mistakes: too many slices, legends far from the ring that force eye travel, and rotating the whole chart while it builds. Spinning donuts look busy and make the angles harder to compare.

moves.name: Map route draw
moves.summary: A route line draws across a map from origin to destination, with a marker leading the line and the camera following the journey.
moves.body:
The route draw shows movement through geography. A line grows along the path, a marker or icon rides its head, and stops can pop in as the line reaches them. On longer journeys the camera pans or zooms to keep the head in frame.

Use it for travel, logistics, delivery, migration, or any story where where-it-went matters. It also works for transit networks, where many routes draw in staggered.

Good practice:

- Mute the base map (low contrast, few labels) so the route is the brightest thing on screen.
- Draw at roughly constant ground speed, then ease out at the destination.
- Drop a short pulse or ring on each stop as the line arrives.
- If the camera moves, ease it on a slightly slower curve than the line so it trails rather than leads.

Common mistakes: straight lines for curved routes, a camera that jumps between zoom levels, and busy map styles that hide the path. Great-circle arcs for flights and real road geometry for drives make it believable.

moves.name: Dot swarm chart
moves.summary: Many small dots, one per unit, fly from a loose cloud into a grid, cluster or scatter plot, so quantities become something you can count.
moves.body:
In a dot swarm, every dot stands for a thing: a person, a million people, a sale. The dots start scattered or piled up, then travel to positions that form a chart. Because the same dots keep moving, they can regroup from one chart to the next and carry the viewer with them.

It shines when scale is the point, or when you want to show the same population sliced several ways.

What makes it work:

- Give each dot a slightly different delay (a few frames of random stagger) so the swarm moves like a flock, not a block.
- Move dots along gentle curves rather than straight lines.
- Color the dots that matter before they move, so the viewer tracks them.
- Say what one dot equals, on screen.

Common mistakes: too many dots to render smoothly, motion so chaotic that nobody sees the final shape, and changing dot meaning between charts. Let the final arrangement hold for a full second before the next regroup.

moves.name: Highlight one bar
moves.summary: After a chart builds, every bar fades to grey except one, which takes the accent color and a label, telling the viewer exactly where to look.
moves.body:
Highlighting one bar is the simplest way to make a chart say one thing. The full chart appears in neutral tones, holds briefly, and then everything except the subject dims while that one bar brightens, maybe grows a little, and gets its value label.

Use it whenever a chart has a hero: your product against competitors, this year against past years, the outlier. It also works on lines, dots and map regions.

How to do it well:

- Build the chart first in one neutral color; the change of color is the moment.
- Dim the others to around 25 to 35% opacity, not zero, so the context stays.
- Add one emphasis only: color, a small lift, or a label. Stacking all three plus a glow is too much.
- Time the highlight on a beat or a spoken word.

Common mistakes: starting with a rainbow chart so the highlight has nothing to contrast against, highlighting several bars at once, and moving the bar so far that the comparison is distorted.

moves.name: Axis and grid reveal
moves.summary: The chart frame builds before the data: axes extend from the origin, gridlines draw across in a quick stagger, and tick labels fade in.
moves.body:
An axis reveal sets the stage for the data. The baseline and vertical axis grow out from their shared corner, faint gridlines unfold across the plot one after another, and tick labels fade in. Only then does the data arrive.

It matters most in explainers, where the viewer needs to know what is being measured before the line or bars appear. In fast promo edits it can be compressed into a quarter of a second.

Keep it subtle:

- Axes are the strongest lines; gridlines sit at low opacity, around 10 to 20%.
- Stagger gridlines from the baseline upward so the build has direction.
- Label units once, clearly, rather than on every tick.
- Leave a short gap before the data starts, so the frame is read as context.

Common mistakes: animating the frame as loudly as the data, rescaling the axis after the data is in place, and decorative tick marks that do not match the real scale. A chart frame that bounces undermines trust in the numbers.

moves.name: Stacked area grow
moves.summary: Layered areas rise from the baseline one band at a time, each stacking on the last, so the viewer sees both the total and its parts.
moves.body:
A stacked area grows each band up from the baseline in turn, or sweeps the whole stack in from left to right. The top edge shows the total; the bands show how it is split and how that split shifts over time.

It works for composition over time: revenue by product, energy mix by source, traffic by channel. Three to five bands is the readable range.

Good choices:

- Put the steadiest band at the bottom so the others have a stable floor.
- Grow bands bottom to top with a short stagger, each rising from the top of the one below it.
- Use related colors with clear value steps, and label bands directly at the right edge instead of in a legend.
- After the build, isolate one band by dimming the rest if there is a point to make.

Common mistakes: animating band heights from zero independently so they overlap, using too many similar colors, and sweeping so fast that the shape change over time is missed. Ease the sweep out so the latest period gets attention.

moves.name: Annotation callout
moves.summary: A leader line draws out from a data point and a short label pops in at its end, pointing the viewer to the one detail that matters.
moves.body:
An annotation callout attaches meaning to a spot on a chart. A small ring pulses on the point, a thin leader line draws out to clear space, and a label with a number or a few words springs in at its end.

Use it for peaks, drops, records, and anything the voiceover names. One callout per moment keeps it clear; if you need several, bring them in one at a time and remove the previous one.

Good practice:

- Draw the leader line from the data point outward, so the eye travels from data to text.
- Keep label text short: a value and two to four words.
- Spring the label in with a small overshoot, then hold still while it is read.
- Place the label where it never covers the data it describes.

Common mistakes: callouts that appear before the data point exists, long sentences in tiny type, and labels that drift with the camera. Give each callout at least a second of hold time per short line of text.

moves.name: Sankey flow
moves.summary: Bands of varying width flow from sources to destinations, drawing left to right so the viewer sees where every share of a total goes.
moves.body:
A Sankey flow shows a total splitting and merging as it moves through stages. Nodes appear as bars on the left, then curved bands draw toward the next column, their widths matching the amounts. The animation turns a dense diagram into a sequence the viewer can follow.

It works for budgets, user funnels, energy use and supply chains, anywhere the question is where does it go.

Making it readable:

- Reveal one stage at a time: nodes, then the bands leaving them, then the next nodes.
- Grow bands along their length (a clip or mask moving left to right), not by fading.
- Color bands by their source so a stream stays identifiable after it splits.
- After the build, light up one path end to end and dim the rest.

Common mistakes: showing all stages at once, too many thin bands that turn into spaghetti, and labels placed on the bands where they collide. Group small flows into an "Other" band and label nodes outside the flow.

moves.name: Before and after data split
moves.summary: Two states of the same chart or metric share the frame, split by a divider that slides across to reveal the change from before to after.
moves.body:
A before and after split puts two versions side by side, or stacked under a moving divider, so the difference is impossible to miss. The divider travels across the frame, revealing the after state behind it, often with the key numbers updating as it passes.

Use it for results: load time before and after, costs before and after, a map in 2000 against 2025. It is strongest when the layout is identical and only the data changes.

What helps:

- Keep axes, scale and framing identical on both sides; otherwise the comparison lies.
- Label each side plainly ("Before" and "After", or the two dates) and keep labels fixed.
- Move the divider with a slow in-out ease, pause in the middle, then finish.
- Finish with the delta as a single number: "-62%" or "3x faster".

Common mistakes: different scales on each side, a divider that moves so fast the before state never registers, and decorative wipes that hide the data. The change should be visible in a still frame.

moves.name: Beat-synced cuts
moves.summary: Scene changes land exactly on the music's downbeats, so the edit feels played by the track instead of laid over it.
moves.body:
Every scene change happens on a measured beat of the song, usually a downbeat. The viewer never sees the sync; they feel that the film and the music are one thing.

It works best for launch films, reels and anything with a clear groove. Big changes (new scene, the reveal, the logo) go on bar 1 of a phrase; smaller changes can sit on beat 3 or on an off-beat for swing.

How to make it hold up:

- Measure the track. Tempo plus first downbeat gives every beat time; guessing drifts by half a second within a minute.
- Cut on the frame closest to the beat. At 30 fps a frame is 33 ms, so rounding is fine; drifting is not.
- Vary the length. Cutting on every single beat for 20 seconds turns into a metronome. Mix 1-, 2- and 4-beat shots.

Common mistakes: syncing to a tempo read off the track's title instead of the audio, starting the music on a pickup note so everything sits a beat late, and fast cuts over text that needs two beats to read.

moves.name: BPM grid timing
moves.summary: All motion durations are written in beats rather than seconds, so every move starts and ends on the song's tempo grid.
moves.body:
Instead of timing an animation in arbitrary milliseconds, you derive every duration from the tempo. At 120 BPM a beat is 500 ms, half a beat 250 ms, a bar 2 s. A card that slides in over one beat and holds for three looks like it belongs to the song even when nothing is cutting.

It is the backbone of any beat-driven piece and also works for silent films: pick a tempo, build the grid, and the rhythm stays consistent across scenes.

How it reads well:

- Start times snap to the grid; durations are whole or half beats.
- Easing still matters. A move that lasts one beat should finish settling on the next beat, not halfway.
- Leave small secondary motions off the grid so the piece breathes.

Common mistakes: snapping everything (it starts to feel mechanical), using a tempo that does not divide cleanly into your frame rate without accounting for rounding, and forgetting that the grid starts at the first downbeat, not at 0 s of the audio file.

moves.name: Kick pulse
moves.summary: An element punches up in scale on every kick drum and eases back before the next one, like it is being pushed by the bass.
moves.body:
A logo, a shape or a whole layer jumps a few percent in size on each kick hit, then relaxes. The attack is instant and the release is slower, which is what makes it read as a hit rather than a wobble.

Use it on drops, chorus sections and end cards, where the music is at full energy. It gives an otherwise static frame a heartbeat.

What makes it work:

- Fast attack, slow release. 1 to 2 frames up, 6 to 10 frames down.
- Small amounts. 3 to 8 percent scale is plenty on a large element. More reads as a glitch.
- Drive it from detected kicks, not from every beat. Many tracks skip kicks in fills and breakdowns, and the pulse should skip with them.

Common mistakes: pulsing text people need to read, scaling from the wrong anchor so the element appears to slide, and running the pulse through quiet sections where there is no kick to justify it. Pair with a brightness bump of a few percent for extra weight.

moves.name: Waveform visualizer
moves.summary: A line traces the actual shape of the audio, scrolling or redrawing each frame so the sound becomes visible.
moves.body:
The waveform visualizer draws the audio signal as a line or a row of mirrored bars. It reads as "this is the sound" more literally than any other visual, which is why it shows up in podcast clips, audiograms and music cards.

There are two main styles:

- **Oscilloscope**: a short window of samples around the current time, redrawn each frame. Lively and jittery.
- **Overview**: the whole clip drawn as an amplitude envelope, with a playhead or fill showing progress. Calm and readable.

When it works: anything where the audio is the product, a voice clip, a song preview, a sound-design reel. It is a weak choice as decoration on a film that is about something else.

Common mistakes: using a random sine wave instead of the real audio (viewers notice it ignores the voice), drawing raw samples without smoothing so it becomes noise at video resolution, and letting the line clip off the top on loud peaks. Normalize to the clip's peak and leave headroom.

moves.name: Frequency bars
moves.summary: A row of bars rises and falls with the music's frequency content, bass on one side and treble on the other.
moves.body:
Frequency bars split the audio into bands and give each band a bar whose height follows its loudness. It is the classic equalizer look, and it reads instantly as music.

It works on music cards, beat-driven reels and anything where you want the track to feel present on screen. It can also be bent into rings, radial bursts or the outline of a logo.

To make it read as real:

- Use a log frequency scale. A linear FFT puts almost all the action in the first few bars.
- Fast rise, slower fall. Bars that jump up in 1 frame and fall over 6 to 10 feel musical; symmetric motion feels like noise.
- Fewer, wider bars read better on video than 256 hairlines. 24 to 64 is a good range.

Common mistakes: fake random bars (they never match a kick, and people notice), no smoothing so bars flicker every frame, and letting the bass bars sit at maximum all the time because the low end was not normalized separately.

moves.name: Lyric sync
moves.summary: Each word of the lyrics appears or highlights exactly when it is sung, timed to the vocal rather than to a guess.
moves.body:
Lyric sync puts the words on screen in step with the singer, word by word or syllable by syllable. Done well, the viewer reads along without effort and the type feels like it is singing.

It is the core of lyric videos and works for spoken word and voiceover captions too.

How to get it right:

- Time from the vocal. Separate the vocal stem, run forced alignment or transcription with word timestamps, then correct by hand where the singer stretches a word.
- Show the line early, highlight the word on time. Readers need the whole line about 300 ms before the first word.
- Give long notes a visible sustain, such as a fill that runs across the word while it is held.

Common mistakes: timing lines off the beat grid instead of the voice (singers are rarely exactly on the beat), revealing words late so the text chases the vocal, and cramming effects through the letters so they stop being readable. Glow and trails belong behind the type.

moves.name: Sound-reactive particles
moves.summary: A particle field breathes with the music: bass pushes it outward, highs add sparkle, and the drop throws it apart.
moves.body:
Here the music drives the parameters of a particle system. Instead of keyframing, you map audio features to forces: low-end energy to expansion, mids to speed or turbulence, high frequencies to brightness or spawn rate, and onsets to bursts.

It is the natural look for music visualizers, VJ-style loops and drop moments in a reel.

What separates good from noisy:

- Map a few features clearly. Three mappings the viewer can feel beat ten they cannot.
- Smooth the inputs. Raw audio features jitter every frame; a short envelope makes the field move like a body.
- Scale reactions by importance: a light nudge on every beat, a strong burst only on the drop or the biggest hits.

Common mistakes: everything reacting at full strength all the time so the frame turns to static, random seeds that change between renders, and reacting to the overall loudness only, which flattens kick, snare and vocal into one blur.

moves.name: Hit frames on transients
moves.summary: Every visible contact, landing or click shares its exact frame with the peak of its sound, so picture and audio feel like one event.
moves.body:
A hit frame is the moment of contact: the ball touches the floor, the card lands, the cursor clicks. A transient is the sharp start of a sound. When the loudest sample of the sound sits on the contact frame, the viewer believes the sound came from the picture.

This matters most for sound effects on UI demos, physics pieces and anything with impacts.

How to place them:

- Measure each sound file's peak offset once (the time from file start to its loudest sample) and schedule it at `contact time − peak offset`.
- One sound per meaningful event. A group of five cards gets one sound, or a sound on the first and last.
- If you cannot be exact, be late, not early. Audio a frame early reads as wrong much sooner than audio a frame late.

Common mistakes: aligning the file start rather than its peak, so every sound lags by its attack time; triggering sounds on animation start instead of contact; and stacking so many effects that none of them read.

moves.name: Silence before the drop
moves.summary: Sound cuts out and the picture freezes or empties for a beat or two, so the next hit lands twice as hard.
moves.body:
A deliberate silence is the most powerful sound in a film. The music drops out, the picture holds still or goes nearly empty, and the viewer leans in. Whatever comes next, the drop or the product name, gets their full attention.

Use it once or twice in a piece: before a drop, before a reveal, or after the final hit as a full stop.

How to make it work:

- Match picture to sound. If audio stops but everything keeps moving, the silence feels like a glitch. Slow or freeze motion with it.
- Keep it short. One or two beats (0.5 to 1 s at 120 BPM) is tension; four seconds is a mistake unless it is the concept.
- Put one thing on screen. A single word, one dot, a cursor hovering.

Common mistakes: fading the music out slowly instead of cutting it (the tension leaks away), leaving room tone or reverb tails that blur the gap, and using the trick so often that it stops surprising.

moves.name: Riser build
moves.summary: Over the bars leading into a drop, motion speeds up, the camera pushes in and the frame tightens until the drop releases it.
moves.body:
A riser is the rising sweep or snare roll producers use to build into a drop. The visual version matches it: over the last 4 or 8 bars before the drop, everything accelerates toward one point.

Typical tools: a slow camera push that speeds up, cuts that halve in length (every 2 beats, then every beat, then every half beat), a light or color that intensifies, and a shape that grows to fill the frame exactly on the drop.

When it works: launch films and reels built on a track with a clear drop. It is the single best way to make the main reveal feel earned.

Common mistakes:

- A linear build. Tension needs an accelerating curve; ease-in, not linear.
- Overshooting the drop. If the build peaks before the drop frame, the drop lands flat. The maximum happens on the drop frame, then releases.
- No release. The frame after the drop should open up, calmer or wider, so the contrast reads.

moves.name: Sidechain pump
moves.summary: Background layers dip in brightness or scale on every kick and swell back between them, mirroring the pumping sound of dance music.
moves.body:
In dance music, sidechain compression makes the pads and bass duck on every kick and swell back in, creating that breathing pump. The visual version does the same thing to the picture: on each kick, background layers dip a little, and they recover before the next one.

It differs from a kick pulse. A pulse pushes the hero element up on the hit; the pump pulls the surroundings down. Used together, the subject seems to punch through the frame.

Best for house, techno and EDM-driven pieces, club visuals and drops.

What makes it convincing:

- The dip is instant and the recovery follows a curve that fills most of the beat, so the frame breathes once per kick.
- Apply it to the background, ambient light or secondary layers, never to text.
- Match depth to the track. A heavily pumped mix can take a 30% brightness dip; a gentle one wants 10%.

Common mistakes: recovering too fast so it looks like a flicker, and pumping during sections without a steady four-on-the-floor kick.

moves.name: Stinger sync
moves.summary: A short, distinct sound plays with a logo lockup so the final frame and the sound resolve together as one signature.
moves.body:
A stinger is a short sound, usually under two seconds, that ends a film or marks a brand moment. The visual lockup and the sound are built as one gesture: the logo arrives on the sting's main hit, and the motion settles as its tail decays.

It works on end cards, channel intros, bumpers and transitions between segments of a series. Reused across videos, it becomes recognizable on its own.

How to build it:

- Design the animation around the sound's envelope. The fastest moment of motion lands on the hit; the slow settle covers the ring-out.
- Keep both short. 1 to 2 seconds total, with a clear final frame held after the sound ends.
- Leave silence after it. A beat of quiet makes the sting read as an ending.

Common mistakes: a sting that peaks while the logo is still moving in, so the hit feels detached; a long tail with nothing on screen; and changing the sting every video so it never becomes a signature.
